stage1.title: CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts documentation poor and not appearing
stage1.body:
## 📚 Documentation

The documentation for the newly introduced `CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts` learning rate scheduler (#17226) does not appear on the website (see [here](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/optim.html); the location where it should be).

Furthermore, looking at the [source code of the function](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/optim/lr_scheduler.py#L699), I am very confused about how to use the scheduler.

Specifically, if we look at the documentation of `.step()`, we first see a clear typo, where `CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts` is called `SGDR`. But the provided example is not sufficient to use as a reference. Where did the value 26 come from and why, and what does it have to do with 10 iterations? Also, [the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03983) on which this scheduler is based states that the LR should be updated every _batch_, not epoch. I believe the statement in the documentation `SGDR.step(0.1), SGDR.step(0.2)` is referring to this, but I am lost in the example.

If I try to ignore the docstring and look at the source code, my best guess is that the correct message for the docstring in `.step` should be something like:

```python
"""Step should be called after every time a batch is processed in addition to after each epoch,
   like in the following example:

         >>> scheduler = CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts(optimizer, T_0, T_mult)
         >>> for epoch in range(N):
         >>>     scheduler.step(epoch)
         >>>     for inputs, labels in trainloader:
         >>>         optimizer.zero_grad()
         >>>         outputs = net(inputs)
         >>>         loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
         >>>         loss.backward()
         >>>         optimizer.step()
         >>>         scheduler.step()
"""
```

Is this correct? Or have I misinterpreted how to apply this function?

Thanks for the great work and please let me know if I can help in some way.

stage3_gold.title: PyTorch issue 20028
stage3_gold.body:
## 📚 Documentation

The documentation for the newly introduced `CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts` learning rate scheduler (#17226) does not appear on the website (see [here](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/optim.html); the location where it should be).

Furthermore, looking at the [source code of the function](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/optim/lr_scheduler.py#L699), I am very confused about how to use the scheduler.

Specifically, if we look at the documentation of `.step()`, we first see a clear typo, where `CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts` is called `SGDR`. But the provided example is not sufficient to use as a reference. Where did the value 26 come from and why, and what does it have to do with 10 iterations? Also, [the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03983) on which this scheduler is based states that the LR should be updated every _batch_, not epoch. I believe the statement in the documentation `SGDR.step(0.1), SGDR.step(0.2)` is referring to this, but I am lost in the example.

If I try to ignore the docstring and look at the source code, my best guess is that the correct message for the docstring in `.step` should be something like:

```python
"""Step should be called after every time a batch is processed in addition to after each epoch,
   like in the following example:

         >>> scheduler = CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts(optimizer, T_0, T_mult)
         >>> for epoch in range(N):
         >>>     scheduler.step(epoch)
         >>>     for inputs, labels in trainloader:
         >>>         optimizer.zero_grad()
         >>>         outputs = net(inputs)
         >>>         loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
         >>>         loss.backward()
         >>>         optimizer.step()
         >>>         scheduler.step()
"""
```

Is this correct? Or have I misinterpreted how to apply this function?

Thanks for the great work and please let me know if I can help in some way.
stage3_gold.comments:
[Kirayue]: Hi, @jcreinhold
I also wondered why it did not appear. Sorry for the poor doc after deciding to change name form SGDR to CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts.
About the usage `LR should be updated every batch, not epoch`, `step()`  without argument is set to epoch update, you can give an argument for a batch update. For example, if you have 15 training examples and batch size is 4, so there would be 4 iterations in an epoch. You could call step(0 + 0 / 4) for the epoch 0 and first batch update, step(0 + 1 / 4) for the epoch 0 and second batch update.
So the code might be modified to 
```
"""Step should be called after every time a batch is processed in addition to after each epoch,
   like in the following example:

         >>> scheduler = CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts(optimizer, T_0, T_mult)
         >>> iters = len(trainloader)
         >>> for epoch in range(N):
         >>>     for i, (inputs, labels) in enumerate(trainloader):
         >>>         scheduler.step(epoch + i / iters)
         >>>         optimizer.zero_grad()
         >>>         outputs = net(inputs)
         >>>         loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
         >>>         loss.backward()
         >>>         optimizer.step()

"""
```

---

[jcreinhold]: @Kirayue I know this is not relevant to the current discussion, but—since you implemented and contributed the method to pytorch—what are your thoughts on adding in "normalized weight decay" as per Appendix B.1 in [Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101), which is, for all intents and purposes, the follow-up paper for SGDR.

They say it is a preliminary result, but "_some_ normalization [on weight decay] can substantially improve results." Any thoughts?

Thanks for the great work and for contributing.

---

[Kirayue]: HI, @jcreinhold
In my opinion, it introduced a new hyperparameter  ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13309212/58142882-5deac780-7c7b-11e9-8ab0-e25ab150361e.png) to replace the original ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13309212/58142910-778c0f00-7c7b-11e9-8923-8ef08272663c.png). And using proposed scaling method to reduce the dependence for weight decay on different computational budgets.
I.e. they use ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13309212/58143193-80311500-7c7c-11e9-96c2-a79837cbdfab.png) to reduce the weight decay and epoch dependence, and they think there might be a better way to do this. ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13309212/58142882-5deac780-7c7b-11e9-8ab0-e25ab150361e.png) is just a new constant. You can take a look at Appendix D.

Please correct me if I am wrong, thank you :smile:

---

[Chillee]: Not all the aspects of this issue have been resolve. For example, it still doesn't show up here: https://pytorch.org/docs/master/optim.html#how-to-adjust-learning-rate.

---

[calincru]: The documentation is still very confusing.  I'm still not sure how it differs from `torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR`.  Is it just the flexibility provided by `T_mult`?  I feel there should be at least some note on this.

Also, slightly related: what I'm interested in is a phase-shifted version of cosine annealing where the training starts with the low learning rates, increases, and then decreases again, and so on (essentially I want the same formula but with `torch.sin` instead of `torch.cos`).  Is it possible to achieve this with one of the existing `CosineAnnealing*` classes?

---

[Kirayue]: Hi, @calincru
The `CosineAnneling` and `Restarts` are both mentioned in [SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03983), so the document looks similar. But the former is more like to [Cyclical Learning Rates](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.01186.pdf). 

BTW, in my opinion, `CosineAnnealing` and `ConsineAnnealingWarmRestarts` are kinds of  `Cyclical LR` (although `CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts` has `T_mult` which makes it not periodic). 

I plot the two lr schedulers on tensorboard, there is a restart point in `CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts` right after reaching the lowest point.
#### CosineAnnealingLR
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13309212/63071590-7acd2900-bf52-11e9-909e-85f67107ee33.png)
#### CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13309212/63071620-9801f780-bf52-11e9-9b68-f84be8e48190.png)

My torch version is 1.1.0.

I think there is no phase or related argument to achieve `sin` but you can modify `CosineAnnealingWarmRestart` code to 
```
def get_lr(self):
    return [self.eta_min + (base_lr - self.eta_min) * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * self.T_cur / self.T_i + math.pi)) / 2 for base_lr in self.base_lrs]
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13309212/63074874-013d3700-bf62-11e9-9f3d-c6a0080b9aca.png)

---

[calincru]: @Kirayue Thanks for clarifications!

---

[peter850706]: Hi, @Kirayue
I read your comments above that mention your torch version is 1.1.0. However, [this warning](https://pytorch.org/docs/master/optim.html#how-to-adjust-learning-rate) indicates that the `scheduler.step()` should be called after `optimizer.step()`.
So I wonder if the example of [CosineAnnealingWarmRestart](https://pytorch.org/docs/master/optim.html#torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts) should be modified as the following:
```
Example:
    >>> scheduler = CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts(optimizer, T_0, T_mult)
    >>> iters = len(dataloader)
    >>> for epoch in range(20):
    >>>     for i, sample in enumerate(dataloader):
    >>>         inputs, labels = sample['inputs'], sample['labels']
    >>>         optimizer.zero_grad()
    >>>         outputs = net(inputs)
    >>>         loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
    >>>         loss.backward()
    >>>         optimizer.step()
    >>>         scheduler.step(epoch + i / iters)
````

---

[AntiLibrary5]: Docs still hasn't been fixed:

https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts.html

stage1.title: `unfold` should not raise such error
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

Based on the document that if `temp = fold(input, ouput_size, **params)` succeeds, `unfold(temp, **params)` will also succeed. So the following code is a bug.

## To Reproduce

```python
import torch
input = torch.rand(torch.Size([1, 12, 12]), dtype=torch.float32)
output_size = [4, 5]
kernel_size = [2, 2]
dilation = 8
padding = 0
stride = 1
res1 = torch.nn.functional.fold(input, output_size, kernel_size, dilation, padding, stride)
res2 = torch.nn.functional.unfold(res1, kernel_size, dilation, padding, stride)
```

`fold` works without error, but `unfold` raises an error:
```
RuntimeError: Given input with spatial size (4, 4), kernel_size=(2, 2), dilation=(8, 8), padding=(0, 0), calculated shape of the array of sliding blocks as (-4, -3), which is too small (non-positive).
```


## Expected behavior

`unfold` does not raise an error.

## Environment

- PyTorch Version (e.g., 1.0): 1.10.0, 1.9.0
- OS (e.g., Linux): Linux
- How you installed PyTorch (conda, pip, source): conda
- Python version: 3.9.5
- CUDA/cuDNN version: 11.1
- GPU models and configuration: RTX 3090


cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @bdhirsh @jbschlosser @albanD @mruberry @walterddr

stage3_gold.comments:
[malfet]: Seems easy to fix, but I guess we need a better audit for those types of errors

---

[malfet]: Though, I guess the question is, what it should return? `nan` as `torch.mean` or exception, as `torch.quantile`

---

[heitorschueroff]: > Though, I guess the question is, what it should return? `nan` as `torch.mean` or exception, as `torch.quantile`

That is an interesting question. I think a more general question is what should we do with reductions over empty slices for operations that don't have an identity. For `mean` and `median` NumPy returns `nan` because these have no identity and the return type is float. For `max` and `min` NumPy raises an error saying these have no identity. For `quantile` NumPy also raises an error but it's not a descriptive one. Finally, `sum` and `prod` have identities so NumPy just returns 0 and 1 respectively. @mruberry  @rgommers do you think we should follow NumPy or always raise an exception for reductions over empty slices without identity? Is this something the Python Array API Standard specifies, or should specify?

---

[rgommers]: > Is this something the Python Array API Standard specifies, or should specify?

It's not specified (yet). I'd like the test suite to cover it. It may be useful to put it in the spec, but I'm not 100% sure - it may be a lot of boilerplate. Perhaps it could be a general design rule somewhere.


> @rgommers do you think we should follow NumPy or always raise an exception for reductions over empty slices without identity

I have the feeling we discussed this somewhere else recently, and the outcome was that an exception should only be raised if no sensible answer is possible. Which is consistent with what NumPy does now.

---

[Jup11ter]: It seems like there is an underlying implementation bug, `torch.nanmedian` also returns `Segmentation fault (core dumped)` in 1.9.0 versions when running the following codes.

In 1.10.0, by contrast, it can run without crashing. I think the reason is that [pr #61698](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/61698) also fixes the bug on `torch.nanmedian`.

```python
import torch

func_cls=torch.nanmedian
t = torch.tensor([])

def test():
	func_cls(t)
test()
```

stage1.title: CUDA error: invalid configuration argument during backward through torch.cdist
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

When back-propagating through torch.cdist operator, the GPU device throws an RuntimeError exception titled:
```
CUDA error: invalid configuration argument.
```

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. create a Python file 'test.py':
```
import torch

for i in range(510, 520):
    a = torch.zeros((4, i, 32)).normal_(0, 1).cuda()
    b = torch.zeros((4, i, 32)).normal_(0, 1).cuda()
    a.requires_grad = True
    b.requires_grad = True
    c = torch.cdist(a, b, p=1.0)
    print(c.size())
```

stage1.title: Current behavior of `as_tuple` argument is inconsistent in `nonzero`
stage1.body:
After `nonzero` started warning that `as_tuple` is a required argument (1.6) a few unfortunate things has happened:
1) the examples in docs started issuing a warning #43425
2) there's no way to pass `out` and `as_tuple` arguments together
```
print(torch.nonzero(a, as_tuple=False)) #ok
print(torch.nonzero(a, out=out)) #warns
print(torch.nonzero(a, as_tuple=False, out=out)) #errors out with `TypeError: nonzero() received an invalid combination of arguments - got unrecognized keyword arguments: out`
```
The rationale behind making `as_tuple` argument required is going through deprecation cycle to change the default value of `as_tuple` so that `torch.nonzero` matches `numpy.nonzero` without any additional args. However, even if implemented properly without problems noted above, this goal is misguided and forces users to modify their codes to avoid warnings for no good reason. 
Torch default behavior for `nonzero` should not match numpy. Numpy behavior can already be achieved by either using `as_tuple=True` or calling `unbind(1)` on results of `torch.nonzero()` call, that is a very light burden for someone who wants it. But to avoid it, we are making everyone who doesn't care jump through deprecation hoops. 
Making numpy behavior default is bad, because numpy returns a tuple of tensors, whereas many users want single tensor return. Going from a single tensor to a tuple is a matter of a cheap `.unbind` call, going from a tuple to a single tensor is memory copy. Default behavior should always pick single tensor. 
My proposal is to go back to making `as_tuple` optional argument and not strive to make `nonzero` match numpy behavior.

cc @albanD @mruberry @rgommers, @alband, @stas00

Going from a single tensor to a tuple is a matter of a cheap `.unbind` call, going from a tuple to a single tensor is memory copy. Default behavior should always pick single tensor. 
My proposal is to go back to making `as_tuple` optional argument and not strive to make `nonzero` match numpy behavior.

cc @albanD @mruberry @rgommers, @alband, @stas00

stage1.title: Better testing on CPUs without AVX capabilities
stage1.body:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/37577 is the latest occurrence of cases where we broke users with non-AVX CPUs because we accidentally let AVX instructions sneak in to code that isn't guarded by DispatchStub. It would be good to actually test for this case.

According to @colesbury, there are no x86 CPUs on AWS that don't support AVX.

Another test we could do is a limited test to see if our static initializers have any AVX instructions, or files that aren't explicitly intended to be AVX/AVX2 compiled. This might be hard to do robustly.

Possibly related https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/22338

cc @malfet @VitalyFedyunin

stage1.title: Running python tests as root breaks the /dev/null file
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

Running python tests as root breaks the `/dev/null` file

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. `su - root`
1. `python3 test/run_tests.py -v -pt`

After that the `/dev/null` file is no longer a character device file but a plain one.

<!-- If you have a code sample, error messages, stack traces, please provide it here as well -->

## Expected behavior

It should not break things of the system.

## Environment

Linux

## Additional context

I've found the root of the problem:

`test_c10d.py` has a test case that creates a `c10d.FileStore("/dev/null", 1)` instance:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/test/distributed/test_c10d.py#L2956

And the `c10d.FileStore` object will remove the file specified by that path upon destruction:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/lib/c10d/FileStore.cpp#L229

Should anyone encountered this issue, it can be fixed by simple re-creating the `/dev/null` file:

```shell
rm -f /dev/null
 mknod -m 666 /dev/null c 1 3
```

cc @pietern @mrshenli @pritamdamania87 @zhaojuanmao @satgera @rohan-varma @gqchen @aazzolini @xush6528 @osalpekar

stage3_gold.comments:
[pranavm-nvidia]: We are running into the same issue - when torch is imported, cuDNN calls from our application are redirected to `libtorch.so` (we looked at a backtrace from `gdb` to confirm this).

---

[zeroepoch]: Any update on this bug?

---

[rmccorm4]: Seeing an issue probably related to this one when importing torch with other GPU-accelerated packages as mentioned above: https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT/issues/317#issuecomment-613716637

---

[mcarilli]: To get more information about what's actually happening, does LD_PRELOAD help?
```
$ LD_PRELOAD=/path/to/preferred/libcudnn.so python script.py
```
?

---

[pranavm-nvidia]: Yes, with LD_PRELOAD it loads the correct cuDNN library, and my application runs without error. 
Without this, I get several cuDNN errors (and in this case, as mentioned before, `gdb` says the functions are in `libtorch.so`)

---

[mcarilli]: > with LD_PRELOAD it loads the correct cuDNN library

Does "it" here mean 
1. Your application
2. The Pytorch internal cudnn calls
3. Both

?  I expect 1, `libtorch.so`'s statically linked internal calls should not be affected by `LD_PRELOAD`.

Do you want Torch-internal calls to use your external cudnn version as well, or do you want the torch-internal calls to continue using `libtorch.so`'s statically linked internal cudnn definitions, while your application uses your external cudnn?

---

[pranavm-nvidia]: Sorry, "it" was referring to my application. 

I just need to make sure my application is using the right cuDNN library; I'm fine with PyTorch using whatever it needs to (presumably what it statically links). 

I think the only thing that needs to be done in PyTorch to fix the issue I see is to hide the cuDNN symbols, either [during linking](https://accu.org/index.php/journals/1372), or afterwards, with something like `strip`

---

[mcarilli]: Pytorch already has [visibility control](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/c10/macros/Export.h) for the functions it defines internally (and therefore probably compiles with `-fvisibility` although I'm not 100% sure of that for the binary builds).  Do you know if we expect compiling `libtorch.so` with `-fvisibility` to hide symbols for externally defined functions, ie, the symbols for the definitions that statically linking against cudnn pulls in?

edit:  after experimenting with minimal examples, it seems compiling and linking a consumer cpp files with `-fvisibility` is _not_ sufficient to hide symbols that are declared in the consumer then statically linked against some other, precompiled static lib.

---

[pranavm-nvidia]: I'm not sure if that's a reliable way to hide symbols from an external, statically linked library. For example, cuDNN might be using visibility attributes, and if you just use `-fvisibility`, I'd imagine that they would be visible in the final library (and they are, as we can see from inspection). 

In fact, it seems that the [linker doesn't impose visibility constraints on static archives](https://stackoverflow.com/a/2251477), so I guess it wouldn't work even if cuDNN doesn't use visibility specifiers.

However, it looks like there's a linker option that can fix this, which might be a lot easier than the solutions I suggested earlier: [-Wl,--exclude-libs](https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Options.html)

---

[mcarilli]: After playing with minimal working samples, if you `-Wl,--exclude-libs,libdummy.a` when creating `libwhatever.so` by linking file(s) including `libdummy.a`, symbols statically linked from `libdummy.a` are hidden in the final `libwhatever.so`, even if `libdummy.a` was compiled with default visibility.

Another working solution is applying pragmas to declarations for symbols you want to hide in consumer (ie Pytorch) cpp files:
```C++
#pragma GCC visibility push(hidden)
#include "cudnn_whatever.h"
#pragma visibility pop
```
Then, even if cudnn is statically linked, and even if the cudnn static library was compiled with default visibility, the resulting `libtorch_whatever.so` should hide the cudnn symbols.  See [here](https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/Visibility), ctrl+f
>#pragma GCC visibility is stronger than -fvisibility; it affects extern declarations as well.

One caveat:  The above reference has some strong warnings about accidentally hiding exception types (ie exceptions that might be thrown by cudnn).  At least I _think_ that's what it's saying, I don't fully understand it.

Two caveat:  the above suggestions are GCC-specific.  I don't know how to rig an equivalent for windows or mac.

---

[pranavm-nvidia]: I don't think cuDNN defines any exceptions, but assuming it did, would PyTorch propagate those (or any other cuDNN types) across its own library boundary? Wouldn't they be caught and handled internally?

If you need more fine-grained control (I don't think you do for cuDNN), a [linker exports map](https://accu.org/index.php/journals/1372) might be the easiest way

---

[mcarilli]: I don't know enough about the build system to decide the right approach here.  I'll ping devs on pytorch slack.

---

[soumith]: `-Wl,exclude-libs` is a reasonable and easy fix, we should do it.

Presumably, has to be inserted here: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/6e4f99b0633f704f8c7bf3bb3b9733680f5dc18b/cmake/public/cuda.cmake#L256-L271

follow along `USE_STATIC_CUDNN=1`

stage1.title: Tensor unfold backward is slow
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

Given the following code, the forward pass is very fast but the backward pass is unreasonably slow. I had a look at the backward pass code and while I am not an expert, I think it could be made significantly faster by writing a custom kernel instead of allocating index arrays, especially since `index_add_` seems to be so slow.

```python
import torch
import time

layer = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 1, 3)
inp = torch.rand(10, 3, 1000, 1000)

out = layer(inp)
c = 5

res = out.unfold(3, c, 1)
res.sum().backward()
```

## 🐛 Bug

Given the following code, the forward pass is very fast but the backward pass is unreasonably slow. I had a look at the backward pass code and while I am not an expert, I think it could be made significantly faster by writing a custom kernel instead of allocating index arrays, especially since `index_add_` seems to be so slow.

```python
import torch
import time

layer = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 1, 3)
inp = torch.rand(10, 3, 1000, 1000)

out = layer(inp)
c = 5

res = out.unfold(3, c, 1)
res.sum().backward()
```

[Coolnesss]: After testing on GPU, if I set the batch size low enough it runs very fast, but anything over 2 and it runs out of memory (8gb GPU). How would I go about debugging the memory usage?

---

[soumith]: the backward pass of an unfold will involved a lot of atomicAdd CUDA instructions in the unfolded dimension. That is what slows down the backward a lot.

---

[Coolnesss]: Hey @soumith, thanks for your reply.

I notice that on GPU the backward pass runs fast but runs out of memory quickly. Do you have any tips on how to check what exactly is being allocated during the backward pass? `nvprof` hangs indefinitely if I run it with `--track-memory-allocations on`.

---

[t-vi]: > Do you have any tips on how to check what exactly is being allocated during the backward pass

I'd look at the [source](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/tools/autograd/templates/Functions.cpp#L640-L652).

I think a better strategy could be to formulate the backward in terms of "source locations", so you'd take a pixel location in the forward's input and sum the gradient entries of the stencil locations where the that input has been mapped to. That should be both relatively efficient in terms of computation (because there won't be conflicting adds) and not need any memory. As a bonus you remove the non-determinism that atomicAdd brings. The disadvantage is that you can't just use unfold to get the indices to add from but have to calculate them yourself, but in 1d that should not be too hard.

---

[Coolnesss]: Hey Thomas, thanks for your reply. 

> The disadvantage is that you can't just use unfold to get the indices to add from but have to calculate them yourself, but in 1d that should not be too hard.

I suppose to calculate the indices one can't just use a for loop in the gradient function, as that wouldn't run on GPU?

---

[t-vi]: Well, if you work out the for loop that iterates over "all output entries y that input entry x will map to in unfold", it's easy to write that for loop in a CUDA kernel and run it in parallel on all your input coordinates.
Let's think about that a moment: So you have at most `ceil(size / step)` entries that any input entry maps to. The first (if any) is at `y = x//step`. Now you have to check `y = x//step ... x//step + ceil(size / step)` whether `y*step <= x < y*step+size`, if it is, add the `gradient_out` at position `y` to the input at `x`. Parallelize using the usual `for (x = threadIdx.x+blockIdx.x ; x < size ; x+= blocksize.x + gridsize.x)` (or so, I forget), and there is the cuda kernel for the backward.
You'd need to double check the above for correctness. Also, I haven't thought about the double backward, through with a bit of luck it's unfold again.

---

[Coolnesss]: @t-vi I could try to make a PR out of this. Do you guys have a guide or some example on how to build PT with the improved backward pass? I've built an extension that uses CUDA using the extensions API, but I guess the process is different for actual internal code.

---

[t-vi]: Thanks!
For general info, there is the [CONTRIBUTING document](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md).
My suggestion would be:
- You'd have to write a new ATen function `unfold_backward`, actually `unfold_backward_cpu` and `unfold_backward_cuda`, probably. You can test those in an extension (that's what I usually do).
Also, I'd write two autogradFunctions `UnfoldFn` and `UnfoldBackwardFn` to see if gradcheck and gradgradcheck (use `UnfoldBackwardFn.apply` and `UnfoldFn.apply` in the backwards) work.
- Maybe `aten/src/ATen/native/TensorTransformations.cpp` and `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/TensorTransformations.cu` are good places for the function. Then add it to `native_functions.yaml` and edit `tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml` (and remove the old backward from `tools/autograd/templates/Functions.cpp`).
- See if you want new tests for it (e.g. test against the current torch_unfold ported back to Python in test/test_torch.py).

Does that make sense, approximately? Don't hesitate to post here if you need feedback or help (link to your git branch if you want to show code).

---

[Coolnesss]: Thanks for the pointers! I'll get to it by first making an extension and testing if it works against the current implementation.

---

[Coolnesss]: Hey, I've made some progress. I have some questions about how to proceed.

What I've done:
* Implemented the new CPU version in C++ for the case where the input is 1D. I've compared it to the existing version and it yields the same results in my tests.
* The algorithm is roughly 
   * Find the first occurence of the input element at index `i` in the output
   * Use some rules to find the next index `j` at which the element appears
   * Add the incoming gradient at index `j` to the outgoing gradient at index `i`

I plan to still:
* Get rid of division and modulo in the algorithm to make it faster
* Implement it in CUDA.

Questions:
* As far as I could tell, I need to know the dimensions of the data at compile time to be able to use accessors. I could create some sort of large if statement for the different input sizes, but it seems like a bad solution. Is there another way, or will I have to deal with strides, etc by using `.data()`?
* I'm a bit confused about the double backward part. Is there something specific that needs to be done in order to support it? Shouldn't it "just work" by calling backward twice?

Thanks for the help so far! Here is the code https://github.com/Coolnesss/unfold-backward/blob/master/unfold.cpp

---

[ezyang]: @Coolnesss awesome!

> As far as I could tell, I need to know the dimensions of the data at compile time to be able to use accessors. I could create some sort of large if statement for the different input sizes, but it seems like a bad solution. Is there another way, or will I have to deal with strides, etc by using .data()?

I'm not 100% familiar with the kernel you're writing. But if you're in a situation where you only care about indexing into, e.g., the last N dimensions (where N is constant), you can just reshape the tensor to have a fixed number of dimensions and then use accessor. Otherwise, you'll have to use one of our classes specifically for arbitrary dimension indexing (but I cannot remember the name right now)

> I'm a bit confused about the double backward part. Is there something specific that needs to be done in order to support it? Shouldn't it "just work" by calling backward twice?

If all operations in backwards are differentiable, it will just work. Otherwise, you'll need to write a derivative for the `unfold_backward` function you wrote.

---

[Coolnesss]: @t-vi, Now that I think about it, doesn't your method of calculating the indices by hand also involve atomicAdds when actually doing the addition? It occured to me that even if one calculates the indices by hand, there's a race condition when adding them since multiple indices of `grad` may point to a single index of `grad_input`. How does one deal with this, or have I misunderstood something?

---

[t-vi]: No, my proposal was to have all writes to one grad_input entry happen in the same thread. Then you don't need atomicAdd. So you'd parallelize the loop over `i` in your code and dimensions `!= dim` (which don't interact). Regarding the problem of Tesor-accessing the right thing: I guess you could either make the thing 3d (`reshape(everything_before_dim, dim, everything_after_dim)`) or do some offset manipulation for the other dimensions and just instantiate a 1-d tensor afterwards.

---

[Coolnesss]: I've made progress yet again. I have the CPU and CUDA implementations done, with the caveat that everything is for the 1D input case only. He's some preliminary benchmarks (on a single RTX 2070)

With the (arbitrarily chosen) parameters
```
input elements = 1e5
dim = 0
size = 10004
step = 3
```

Old backward:
20.4 ms ± 12.9 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
Peak memory usage 3.60 gb

New backward:
13.6 ms ± 15.4 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
Peak memory usage 1.20 gb

Next up:
* I believe I will need some help in handling the N-D input case. In the actual CUDA kernel I will have to deal with strides etc myself so what is the best way of implementing this? Actually I'm not too sure how to calculate the gradient in this case.
* The double backward needs to be written. I guess I have to write another kernel, but do I also write another `torch.autograd.function`? How does this work in terms of the extension?

---

[t-vi]: Good job!
- For the N-D case in cuda, one thing you can do is to mimic what [OffsetCalculator](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/cuda/detail/OffsetCalculator.cuh) does. Not in the sense of the actual computation, but pass in strides and sizes as arrays as fixed-size array (MAX_DIMS is 25 for OffsetCalculator). Then you can just multiply up the position from a linear index. (You could see if you can use OffsetCalculator itself for the initial offset. If not, the division-avoiding computation probably isn't as important.)
- I think you need to differentiate between 32 and 64 bit arithmetic. See e.g. batch norm for how to do that with ATen's utility function.
- I think the double backward is just fold again. To check this, define an `UnfoldBackwardFunction` and use that in the `FoldFunction` backward instead of calling unfold_backward directly. Then in the forward of the `UnfoldBackwardFunction` use the `unfold_backward` you have and in the backward use FoldFunction.apply again. Doing this consistently (i.e. making all indexing, looping use an `typename index_t` template parameter and specializing to int64_t or int32_t) might also give you a speed up in the 32bit case over mixing 32 and 64 bit indexing.

Later, you should probably change the checking etc to the C++ style of ATen.

---

[dangpzanco]: any update on this issue?

---

[ezyang]: paging @albanD who has been doing a lot of work on unfold recently

---

[nikitaved]: Any update? I could have a look at this one...

---

[albanD]: I don't think anyone is looking into this.
It most likely requires to write a specialized cuda kernel to replace the current implementation that call many different kernels.

---

[paplhjak]: I for one would appreciate it, as it would help tremendously with speed of training networks with spatially variant convolution kernels.

---

[nikitaved]: OK, them I will look into it as soon as I get time. Meanwhile, if someone interested, please, feel free to assign yourself!

---

[ngimel]: @paplhjak is it for cpu or gpu? Also it would be helpful if you provided some representative parameters for benchmarking.

---

[nikitaved]: All right, it seems like we have at most `floor((size - 1) / step)` overlaps in each slice with the right/left neighbor slice . Hence it is easy to tell whether a CUDA index might have a potential overlap with any other index in any slice of size `size`, call it a "problematic" index if there is an overlap. My plan of attack is to leave everything to operate over 1D tensors, as it is right now before `index_add`, but replace `index_add` with a kernel which performs a simple assignment for "good" indices, and an atomic add for "problematic" indices. 
Do you agree with this approach? Could you please share you suggestions as to how to organize the code (I guess it will require specifying the function inside the `native_functions.yaml`?)? This approach can be easily extended to CPU without `index_add`.

[nikitaved]: @Coolnesss , could you please share your benchmarking scripts for my own testing? Thank you!

[t-vi]: @nikitaved A long time ago (see the discussion above) my impression was that it'd be preferable to just parallelize over the `grad_in`, i.e. the have one thread process each backward kernel output (or several outputs in a for loop). That way you'd have many reads (hopefully hitting caching), but the minimal number of writes and no need for atomicAdd at all.

---

[nikitaved]: @t-vi , thank you for your comment! I agree with your approach and I will give it a try.
I would also like to see some generic use cases for this function, just to see what kind of overlap patters are expected.

[Coolnesss]: Hey guys, sorry for leaving this thing, I haven't had time to work on it for a while. 

@nikitaved here's the repository I made when I worked on this (https://github.com/Coolnesss/unfold-backward) there's a few benchmarks and some code as well. Hope it helps.

[t-vi]: I don't know, people tend to have use cases beyond my imagination.
If you want, you could use a pattern where the threads each take of writing some zeros and then taking care of a potential non-zero. I think it should work well even if it complicates the block/grid layout calculation by a small bit.
I would likely try to have a single integrated kernel that covers both cases. Saves headache and you don't have to think of the decision which to use.

Overall, parallelization over the output is beneficial for small values of `c` and small values of `step`, however it is slower for cases with large `c` and small `step`.
Hence for small values of `c` and small `step` the parallelization over the output of the backward method is better (about 25% faster), for other cases the parallelization over input is more efficient. I will show the exact numbers later.

stage1.title: Singular value decomposition of complex valued matrices does not match mathematical definition
stage1.body:
## 📚 Documentation

Now when `torch.svd` supports complex input both for CPU and CUDA. Let's discuss the docs.
Currently, SVD documentation is fully in agreement with the implementation. This function returns`(U, S, V)` such that `input = U @ diag(S) @ V.T`
However, the mathematical definition of SVD is the decomposition of a matrix **M** such that ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/19621411/95017939-e72e4e80-0664-11eb-8efe-a853724d142a.png), where `V^*` is the conjugate transpose of `V`. 

What is the opinion on this? Should the documentation and implementation match math and be updated such that `A = U @ diag(S) @ V.T.conj()`?

[Link to `torch.svd` documentation](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.svd.html).



cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @bdhirsh @heitorschueroff @anjali411 @dylanbespalko @mruberry @jlin27 @vishwakftw @jianyuh @nikitaved @pearu @vincentqb

Now when `torch.svd` supports complex input both for CPU and CUDA. Let's discuss the docs.
Currently, SVD documentation is fully in agreement with the implementation. This function returns`(U, S, V)` such that `input = U @ diag(S) @ V.T`
However, the mathematical definition of SVD is the decomposition of a matrix **M** such that ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/19621411/95017939-e72e4e80-0664-11eb-8efe-a853724d142a.png), where `V^*` is the conjugate transpose of `V`. 

What is the opinion on this? Should the documentation and implementation match math and be updated such that `A = U @ diag(S) @ V.T.conj()`?

[Link to `torch.svd` documentation](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.svd.html).



cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @bdhirsh @heitorschueroff @anjali411 @dylanbespalko @mruberry @jlin27 @vishwakftw @jianyuh @nikitaved @pearu @vincentqb
stage3_gold.comments:
[pearu]: xref: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/45063 - conjugate transpose operator feature request

---

[pearu]: IIUC, the current SVD documentation uses transpose because previously only real input was supported (and hence using conjugate transpose would have been unnecessary). With the new complex input support in SVD, I would suggest updating the SVD documentation to use conjugate transpose to match the mathematical definition of general SVD. While doing so, also mention that when M is real then V will be real and conjugate transpose falls back to transpose.

---

[ezyang]: Yes, please just generalize the docs, in this case it seems to be straightforward and the right thing to do.

---

[nikitaved]: The current SVD implementation returns `V` that is silently conjugated. I guess it makes sense to fix that too, is that correct?

---

[mruberry]: > The current SVD implementation returns `V` that is silently conjugated. I guess it makes sense to fix that too, is that correct?

As far as I understand what you're saying: yes.

---

[antocuni]: I'd like to add my 2 cents to this discussion. By looking at the source code, it seems to me that the current behavior or `torch.svd` was not designed, but simply a byproduct of a bug. In particular, look at `_create_U_S_VT`:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a814231616f5db7fcdb8793f64c12d652d1e8572/aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebraUtils.h#L221

As the name suggests, it should create a `VT` tensor, which is done here:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a814231616f5db7fcdb8793f64c12d652d1e8572/aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebraUtils.h#L246-L247

However, the comment is wrong: the lapack's function `_gesdd` returns a `VT` in *column-major* order.

The rest of the code keeps calling it `VT`; e.g., this is `_svd_helper_cpu` returning a tuple `(U, S, VT)`:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a814231616f5db7fcdb8793f64c12d652d1e8572/aten/src/ATen/native/BatchLinearAlgebra.cpp#L1058

However, since we are creating the tensor with the wrong strides, we are effectively returning `VT.transpose()`, which is `V`. To summarize:
* `numpy.linalg.svd` returns `VT`
* lapack retusn `VT`
* our implementation returns something which is called `VT` (but it's not)

So, it looks to me that the intention was to return `VT` as well, but because of the bug in `_create_U_S_VT`, we started to return `V` and instead of fixing the bug we simply "fixed" the documentation.

There isn't much that we can to at this point without breaking compatibility, but this confusing/unexpected/nonstandard behavior of `svd` might indicate that we should deprecate it in favor or `torch.linalg.svd`, once it lands.

Note: in my WIP PR #45562 I fixed `_create_U_S_VT` by creating `VT` with the correct strides, and `transpose_()`ing it upon return to keep b/c.
In the same PR I am also going to fix the docs for `torch.svd`.

---

[mruberry]: Sounds great, @antocuni! I agree we should consider deprecating torch.svd once torch.linalg.svd lands. It will also be confusing to have a method torch.Tensor.svd when both functions are in because users may not know which svd it refers to.

---

[antocuni]: > It will also be confusing to have a method torch.Tensor.svd when both functions are in because users may not know which svd it refers to.

This is something which I didn't think about. What should `Tensor.svd` do if/when we remove `torch.svd`? Ideally it would do the same as `torch.linalg.svd`, but this will break compatibility.

> In the same PR I am also going to fix the docs for torch.svd.

FWIW, this is the commit which aims to fix the documentation:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/45562/commits/97662da54aba366dd547e46d557edc2b86ff86dc

---

[mruberry]: > > It will also be confusing to have a method torch.Tensor.svd when both functions are in because users may not know which svd it refers to.
> 
> This is something which I didn't think about. What should `Tensor.svd` do if/when we remove `torch.svd`? Ideally it would do the same as `torch.linalg.svd`, but this will break compatibility.

We should warn/deprecate for a release and then remove both functions for a release. Then we can consider adding torch.Tensor.svd back and mapping it to torch.linalg.svd.

---

[antocuni]: (sorry guys, I closed the issue by mistake, reopening it)

---

[pulkin]: You probably do know that `numpy` returns `u, s, vh = svd(A)` such that `A = u @ s @ vh`. I would prefer to have this convention in `pytorch` because many people use `numpy` for prototyping.

---

[antocuni]: while working on PR #45562 we realized that we can't fix `torch.svd` without breaking existing code. OTOH, the upcoming `torch.linalg.svd` is completely compatible with numpy.
As discussed on the PR, the current plan is to document the current behavior of `torch.svd` and tell people to use `torch.linalg.svd` for new code: this is the commit which tentatively tries to improve the docs, but feel free to suggest a better wording:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/45562/commits/abf9baffc200ac6a459e78c70ce5e5c05594608e

stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

Per title

Currently, we directly `copy_` the result into the output tensor.
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/d490e0120f32dcbb8b23e11eebd638b96b4b0898/aten/src/ATen/native/Linear.cpp#L644
If the output tensor can be broadcasted from result, it would generate wrong output.

## To Reproduce

```py
>>> a = torch.randn(5)
>>> b = torch.randn(5)
>>> torch.inner(a, b)
tensor(-4.2595)
>>> c = torch.randn(2)
>>> torch.inner(a, b, out=c)
tensor([-4.2595, -4.2595])
```

## Expected
```py
>>> a = torch.randn(5)
>>> b = torch.randn(5)
>>> torch.inner(a, b)
tensor(-4.2595)
>>> c = torch.randn(2)
>>> torch.inner(a, b, out=c)  # c should be resized to shape([1])
tensor([-4.2595])
```

stage1.title: [Discussion] Implement sth like torch_global_deps on Windows
stage1.body:
## What is wrong there?
In https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/torch-cat-runtimeerror-error-in-loadlibrarya/71188/5, we can see that it is caused by the fact that `caffe2_nvrtc.dll` is not loaded during initialization. Currently, it will only happen when one trys to use CUDA in the official distribution of Python 3.8. It doesn't apply the changes to `PATH` for DLL search purposes, which makes  `caffe2_nvrtc.dll`  not able to found during runtime.

## Possible solutions
1. Load `caffe2_nvrtc.dll` when possible during initialization.  This is a quick fix, which is not so general.
2. Write the dependencies to a text file and load them one by one during initialization.
3. Load torch_global_deps during initialization. However, there is currently no easy way to force linking against unused shared libraries unless we use sth like `/INCLUDE:[symbol_name]`. Related PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/34288.
4. Load all DLLs in the lib directory (Looks like a decent solution)

cc @peterjc123 @ezyang @malfet @EscapeZero @kostmo @soumith

stage1.title: Use of Tensor.contiguous() unconditionally results in Mypy linting errors
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

In `tools/pyi/gen_pyi.py` there is no type hint provided for `Tensor.contiguous()` (`Tensor.is_contiguous()` is there however).  As a result uses of `.contiguous()` cause Mypy linting errors.  

In the case I had the line (the context and details of the tensors doesn't matter):

```
re_batched = seq_first.contiguous().view(expanded_tokens.size(1), -1).transpose(0, 1)
```

gives the linting error:

```
error: "Tensor" has no attribute "contiguous"; maybe "is_contiguous"?
```

## To Reproduce

Any use of `Tensor.contiguous` will produce this when linted with MyPy

## Expected behavior

No error should be reported

stage1.title: Suggest adding the words 'Chi-squared' to the docstring of the Chi2 distribution to be explicit
stage1.body:
## 📚 Documentation

The [documentation on this](http://deepmind.github.io/torch-distributions/#toc_29) is fine but I suggest that the docstring information attached to the [`Chi2`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c371542efc31b1abfe6f388042aa3ab0cef935f2/torch/distributions/chi2.py) object should include the words 'Chi-squared' or 'Chi squared'.  Simply saying 'creates a Chi2 distribution' did not give me the confidence that `Chi2` was in fact the chi-squared distribution.  I don't think 'chi2' is universally understood as 'chi-squared'.  Wikipedia, Khan Academy, and other texts I looked at did not use the term 'chi2'.

```
[docs]class Chi2(Gamma):
    r"""
    Creates a Chi2 distribution parameterized by shape parameter :attr:`df`.
    This is exactly equivalent to ``Gamma(alpha=0.5*df, beta=0.5)``

    Example::

        >>> m = Chi2(torch.tensor([1.0]))
        >>> m.sample()  # Chi2 distributed with shape df=1
        tensor([ 0.1046])

    Args:
        df (float or Tensor): shape parameter of the distribution
    """
    
```

I think this is the docstring in question:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c371542efc31b1abfe6f388042aa3ab0cef935f2/torch/distributions/chi2.py#L7-L8

cc @brianjo @mruberry

stage1.title: Python 3.9 installs torch to a wrong version if git commit starts with '0'
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

Probably not a big issue, but an interesting one.

In python 3.9, when a torch git commit starts with '0', e.g. `0567988`, a `python setup.py install` would install it to a version of `1.9.0a0+567988` with the leading 0 removed.

A python warning message like this is printed

```
Building wheel torch-1.9.0a0+0567988
/usr/lib/python3.9/site-packages/setuptools/dist.py:452: UserWarning: Normalizing '1.9.0a0+0567988' to '1.9.0a0+567988'
  warnings.warn(tmpl.format(**locals()))
```

The version in pip freeze is "wrong",

```
$ pip freeze | grep -i torch
torch==1.9.0a0+567988
```

but the version in `torch.__version__` is correct

```
$ python -c 'import torch; print(torch.__version__)'                    
1.9.0a0+0567988
```

stage3_gold.title: PyTorch issue 52857
stage3_gold.body:
## 🐛 Bug

Probably not a big issue, but an interesting one.

In python 3.9, when a torch git commit starts with '0', e.g. `0567988`, a `python setup.py install` would install it to a version of `1.9.0a0+567988` with the leading 0 removed.

A python warning message like this is printed

```
Building wheel torch-1.9.0a0+0567988
/usr/lib/python3.9/site-packages/setuptools/dist.py:452: UserWarning: Normalizing '1.9.0a0+0567988' to '1.9.0a0+567988'
  warnings.warn(tmpl.format(**locals()))
```

The version in pip freeze is "wrong",

```
$ pip freeze | grep -i torch
torch==1.9.0a0+567988
```

but the version in `torch.__version__` is correct

```
$ python -c 'import torch; print(torch.__version__)'                    
1.9.0a0+0567988
```

Theoretically, this behavior will trigger with an odd of 1 in 16. 🤔

cc @malfet @seemethere @walterddr @albanD
stage3_gold.comments:
[albanD]: cc @malfet what do you think should be the priority here?

---

[malfet]: Hmm, if I understand what is going on, it should be much more rare:  `0567988` is at some point is interpreted as number rather than string, but I guess this would only hold true for short hexadecimal hashes that do not contain hexadecimal digits. 
It potentially can get even weirder if all digits would be less than 8, because then it might potentially be interpreted as octal number (by C)

I think it's a low pri, but should be pretty easy to fix

---

[walterddr]: "Good first issue" tag probably?

---

[malfet]: This is a way to reproduce the problem: `python3 -c "from setuptools.extern import packaging;print(packaging.version.Version('1.2.3+002345'))"`

 https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0440/#local-version-identifiers says the following about stripping leading zeros from the local version:
> If a segment consists entirely of ASCII digits then that section should be considered an integer for comparison purposes

stage3_gold.comments:
[xush6528]: Motivation

* It is causing RPC C++ entries to return different types, RPC TorchScript returns ivalue::Future. This is blocking Dist autograd Profiler(Rohan) and adding Future Python Type Annotation(Wanchao, Shihao).
* Autograd, DistAutograd, RPC is using utils::Future<T>, while JIT/TorchScript is using ivalue::Future. On integration point of RPC and JIT modules, this always creates divergent code paths and inconvenience for developers.

Plan

* Wrap utils::Future<rpc::Message> returned by RPC Python/BuiltinOp code paths into ivalue::Future[PyObject]. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/35154
* Make ivalue::Future behave not exactly the same as utils::Future<T>. There are a few differences now. Will change them to the same behavior before replace ivalue::Future with utils::Future<IValue>. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/35849
    * ivalue::Future::wait() only waits, does not returns value.
    * ivalue::Future::value() always returns a copy.  While utils::Future<T> wait() returns a reference.
    * ivalue::Future::FutureError and utils::FutureError are 2 types.
    * ivalue::Future::markCompleted takes FutureError. utils::Future<T>::setError takes FutureError.
    * ivalue::Future::addCallback adds a lambda that takes no argument. utils::Future<T>::addCallback adds a lambda that takes T and FutureError.
    * ivalue::Future assumes the value is default construct-able, so it can mark future as completed without providing value.
    * ivalue::Future support stream operator

---

[pritamdamania87]: @xush6528 Thanks for all the work on this! Since https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/35849 and https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/35154 are closed, could you update this issue with any outstanding items that we still need to address?

---

stage1.title: Segmentation fault in DataLoader worker in PyTorch 1.8.0 if set_num_threads is called beforehand
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

A segmentation fault occurs if one uses `DataLoader` with `num_workers` > 0 after calling `set_num_threads` with a sufficiently high value.
I observed this behaviour in PyTorch 1.8.0 and 1.8.1, but I am unable to reproduce it with PyTorch 1.7.1.

## To Reproduce

```
import torch

def main():
    torch.set_num_threads(4)

    dataloader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader([1, 2, 3], num_workers=1)
    iter(dataloader).next()

    return

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

The above code crashes when `set_num_threads` is called with 4 or more as its argument.
Incidentally (or maybe not) 4 is the number of vCPUs in the AWS EC2 instance I am using.

## Expected behavior

No crash.

model_evidence.title: Segmentation fault in DataLoader worker in PyTorch 1.8.0 if set_num_threads is called beforehand
model_evidence.body:
## 🐛 Bug

A segmentation fault occurs if one uses `DataLoader` with `num_workers` > 0 after calling `set_num_threads` with a sufficiently high value.
I observed this behaviour in PyTorch 1.8.0 and 1.8.1, but I am unable to reproduce it with PyTorch 1.7.1.

## To Reproduce

```
import torch

def main():
    torch.set_num_threads(4)

    dataloader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader([1, 2, 3], num_workers=1)
    iter(dataloader).next()

    return

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

The above code crashes when `set_num_threads` is called with 4 or more as its argument.
Incidentally (or maybe not) 4 is the number of vCPUs in the AWS EC2 instance I am using.

## Expected behavior

No crash.

stage1.title: optimize_for_mobile segfaults during forward of mobilenet_v3
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

Applying `optimize_for_mobile` into a `mobilenet_v3` from torchvision leads to a segfault on the 3rd forward pass.

## To Reproduce

```python
import torch, torchvision
from torch.utils.mobile_optimizer import optimize_for_mobile

m = torchvision.models.mobilenet_v3_large()
m = torch.jit.script(m)
m = optimize_for_mobile(m)

# run forward 3 times until segfault
m(torch.rand(1, 3, 224, 224))
m(torch.rand(1, 3, 224, 224))
m(torch.rand(1, 3, 224, 224))
```
yielding
```
Segmentation fault: 11
```

I'm using PyTorch `1.8.0.dev20210125` with latest torchvision.

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @bdhirsh @jbschlosser

model_evidence.title: optimize_for_mobile segfaults during forward of mobilenet_v3
model_evidence.body:
## 🐛 Bug

Applying `optimize_for_mobile` into a `mobilenet_v3` from torchvision leads to a segfault on the 3rd forward pass.

## To Reproduce

```python
import torch, torchvision
from torch.utils.mobile_optimizer import optimize_for_mobile

m = torchvision.models.mobilenet_v3_large()
m = torch.jit.script(m)
m = optimize_for_mobile(m)

# run forward 3 times until segfault
m(torch.rand(1, 3, 224, 224))
m(torch.rand(1, 3, 224, 224))
m(torch.rand(1, 3, 224, 224))
```
yielding
```
Segmentation fault: 11
```

I'm using PyTorch `1.8.0.dev20210125` with latest torchvision.

[apaszke]: My guess would be that one of the workers quit before the main process has managed to receive some tensors form it.

---

[jfsantos]: Yes, that could be the case, since I'm doing some expensive operations inside that loop. Is there any way of specifying a timeout for the workers?

---

[apaszke]: No, there's not, but it should be unnecessary. They should be stopped only once the main process receives and returns all batches. What arguments did you pass in to the DataLoader constructor (other than the dataset)?

---

[jfsantos]: I'm using `batch_size=1, collate_fn=MyDataset.collate_samples, num_workers=1, shuffle=False`. The `collate_samples` function is only used to concatenate things that are not tensors.

---

[apaszke]: It would be great if you could try to get us a small script that would reproduce it. I'm only afraid that it might be caused by some specific case of interleaving subprocess execution, that will be different on our hardware. But should be worth trying anyway 😕

---

[jfsantos]: I kind of worked around this by setting `num_workers=0` until now since I was only having the issue during test time, but now I started seeing this during validation, which is pretty bad. I will try to reproduce it and will let you know if I manage to do it.

---

[skaae]: I have the same problem. I can get rid of the problem by having my collate_fn return numpy arrays instead of Torch tensors. I.e. commenting the `from_numpy` lines removes the problem. I also get the problem if i create the tensor with `torch.FloatTensor(some_np_arr)`. 

```Python
    @staticmethod
    def collate_fn(batch):
        org_audio_len_lst, audio_lst, spec_linear_lst, spec_mel_lst, speaker_class_lst, sample_info_lst = zip(*batch)
        audio_arr = np.stack(audio_lst,0).astype('float32')
        spec_linear_arr = np.stack(spec_linear_lst, 0).astype('float32')
        spec_mel_arr = np.stack(spec_mel_lst, 0).astype('float32')

        audio_arr = torch.from_numpy(audio_arr)    
        spec_linear_arr = torch.from_numpy(spec_linear_arr)
        spec_mel_arr = torch.from_numpy(spec_mel_arr)
        speaker_class_tensor = torch.LongTensor(speaker_class_lst)
        return {'audio': audio_arr, 'spec_linear': spec_linear_arr, 'spec_mel': spec_mel_arr,
                'speaker_class': speaker_class_tensor}

```

---

[apaszke]: That's because numpy arrays are pickled and unpickled instead of using shared memory. There are probably very tight limits on the shared memory size in your systems, or the workers quit in a weird way. Does it happen at the end of an epoch?

---

[skaae]: Ok. 
It always happens after the same number of batches have been loaded from disk. like i'm hitting some limit.

In my setup I load 512 samples to memory at the beginning of training. The samples are stored in list. 
The 512 samples in memory are periodically replaced randomly with new samples loaded from disk. 

Is that the problem and do you have workaround ? :)

---

[apaszke]: No, I could never reproduce that so I need more information. How many batches can you load until this happens, and how many batches does your dataset has in total?

[skaae]: Sorry about the vaque description. I'll try to create a minimal example tomorrow and post it here.

---

[sampathweb]: Increasing the `ulimit` solved the issue.  Details (https://github.com/fastai/fastai/issues/23).  When using Docker, the `ulimit` is set very high so you may never see the issue, but Ubuntu instance by default had 1024 (file descriptor limit).  Increasing it to 2048 or 4096 or higher solves the issue.  I don't know why that many file descriptors are required, but glad that it had a simple fix.

---

[sampathweb]: If the core devs want to see the error, just reduce the `ulimit` to 1024 and run the code of @kamo-naoyuki above and you might see the same problem.

---

[jph00]: This does seem to be an issue in pytorch as best as we can tell - FDs aren't being released when they should be. As @sampathweb mentioned, it's reproducible using the above code. The workaround for now is:

```
import resource
rlimit = resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE)
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE, (2048, rlimit[1]))
```
(You may need to set 2048 to a higher number.)

---

[apaszke]: And if you can't change the limits because you don't have super user access, you can always switch to [file name based IPC](http://pytorch.org/docs/master/multiprocessing.html#file-system-file-system).

---

[jph00]: BTW we fixed this problem (and got a good speedup, and also fixed some occassional multiprocessing hangs) in fastai by switching to ThreadPool. Requires libs that release the GIL of course, but opencv does that. :)

---

[apaszke]: Yeah I saw that. I don't think we will want to do this in general, as some datasets might be more GIL-heavy and this would have a huge perf hit, but an option that makes the data loader use threads instead of subprocesses should be quite easy to implement.

---

[apaszke]: Tensors are always passed through shared memory. Try switching to the file name based sharing, or increase the limit of file descriptors per process using `ulimit`

[Avsecz]: @ivanprado great catch. In my case, this occurred during test-time since I was keeping track of the target values from all the batches (hence many shared objects had to be tracked). I solved the problem by copying the objects using `copy.deepcopy` and removing the shared objects. This doesn't happen during training time since the targets get discarded right after the SGD update (hence only a few shared objects need to be tracked).

Here is my solution

```python
from copy import deepcopy

pred_list = []
target_list = []
# long version
for inputs, targets in DataLoader(dataset, num_workers=6, batch_size=64):
    pred_list.append(model.predict_on_batch(inputs))  # make model prediction
    targets_copy = deepcopy(targets)
    target_list.append(targets_copy)
    del inputs
    del targets

# short version. interpreter invokes `del` automatically for inputs and targets
for inputs, targets in DataLoader(dataset, num_workers=6, batch_size=64):
    pred_list.append(model.predict_on_batch(inputs))  # make model prediction
    target_list.append(deepcopy(targets))  # append targets copy. `targets` removed automatically
```

Doing so, I was able to run the code without `torch.multiprocessing.set_sharing_strategy('file_system')`.

[Baranowski]: I reproduced the `received 0 items of ancdata` error but couldn't reproduce the FD leak that IvanPrado diagnosed (except the expected scenario where references to the SHM tensors are kept alive outside the DataLoader loop). I think it's fair to ignore the latter part of this issue unless it's observed in the wild again. My rationale:

* It's been almost 2 years so even if there was a bug causing leaks in PyTorch, it might have been fixed since.
* It's possible that the user's code was keeping the SHM tensors alive longer than necessary by maintaining reference to them outside the DataLoader loop. (To be fair, I didn't find any such mistake reading his code, or any other proof of that, but it's possible that we have both missed something.)

If we agree to disregard the report of FD leaks, this issue is reduced to the obscure `RuntimeError: received 0 items of ancdata` exception that the users see.

(**Suggestion 1**) IMO the best improvement would be for the parent process to report the stderr of the crashed workers (or to wrap the worker in a try...catch that gracefully kills the worker and somehow reports the exception back to the parent).

(**Suggestion 2**) It might be also useful to warn the user when a SHM tensor outlives the DataLoader's itearator's iteration. I'm not sure how doable that is with the Python's GC though..

The obscure error `RuntimeError: received 0 items of ancdata` is not a good user experience but it's not terrible since typing it into Google leads to a lot of pages with the workaround that's easily applied. As much as I would like to work on Suggestion 1, perhaps the `high priority` label should be reconsidered at a triage meeting.

stage1.title: HalfCauchy does not respect _validate_args
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

The `validate_args` argument to a `torch.distribution.Distribution`'s constructor should enable support checking for a distribution. This works fine for Beta and Bernoullii distributions, but `HalfCauchy` does not throw a run-time exception when support checking fails.

## To Reproduce

When I run `torch.distributions.HalfCauchy(1.0, validate_args=True).log_prob(torch.tensor(-1))`, no run-time error is thrown, but a -inf log prob is returned.

## Expected behavior

Same behavior as Bernoulli; a `ValueError` for the failed support check.

stage1.title: Support CUDA and backpropagation in `torch.orgqr`
stage1.body:
## 🚀 Feature

As of PyTorch 1.7, `torch.orgqr` only supports CPU tensors and does not implement gradients. 
Feature proposal: add support for CUDA tensors and gradients wrt inputs.

## Motivation

<!-- Please outline the motivation for the proposal. Is your feature request related to a problem? e.g., I'm always frustrated when [...]. If this is related to another GitHub issue, please link here too -->

This function is required to perform orthogonal parameterization of matrices (not to be confused with orthogonal initialization). Given an input matrix of shape `d x r` with `d >= r`, `orgqr` produces an orthogonal matrix of the same shape `d x r`. The output spans the manifold of Stiefel frames of size `d x r`, and hence, provides precise orthogonal constraints by construction. This can be used further, e.g. as a weight matrix in an RNN transition layer or any other place requiring strict orthogonality. More motivation can be found here and references therein: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/42243
Without GPU, the function is slow. Without gradients, parameterization becomes impossible. Once the requested feature is implemented, and once this PR https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/33344 is merged, it will become possible to perform precise orthogonal parameterization of weight matrices in Linear, all flavors of Convolutional, and Embedding layers.

## Pitch

<!-- A clear and concise description of what you want to happen. -->

`torch.orgqr` to support the two requested properties.
As hinted by @Lezcano, MAGMA already implements a GPU side of the function: https://www.icl.utk.edu/~mgates3/docs/magma-proto.html
The gradients can be taken from my package https://github.com/toshas/torch-householder/blob/master/torch_householder/householder.cpp#L58

## Alternatives

The code from my package https://github.com/toshas/torch-householder implements an efficient drop-in replacement for `torch.orgqr` satisfying the requested properties, and I don't mind donating this code. The forward pass might be slower than that of MAGMA -- no comparison was done.

## Additional context

<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->

None so far

stage1.title: Complex dtype and named tensors don't go along
stage1.body:
## 🚀 Feature
Support differentiation for complex-valued named tensors.



## Motivation
Complex datatypes and named tensors are an important (yet experimental) feature yey `view_as_complex` and `view_as_real` will not support differentiation of complex tensors.

**Problem:**
```
import torch
names = ["batch", "height", "width", "complex"]
z = torch.ones((5, 12, 14, 2), requires_grad=True).refine_names(*names)
z_complex = torch.view_as_complex(z.rename(None)).refine_names(*names[:-1])
```
Results in:

`RuntimeError: alias does not support automatic differentiation for outputs with complex dtype.
`

There is no hope in building such a function yourself either:
```
def view_as_complex(data):
    """Named version of `torch.view_as_complex()`"""
    data = data.clone()
    real_part = data[..., 0]
    imag_part = data[..., 1]

    return (real_part + 1j*imag_part).refine_names(*data.names[:-1])
```
gives the same error.


## Additional context
PyTorch 1.7 however introduces complex-valued spectral operators, requiring code that uses channels to represent real and imaginary parts to use `view_as_complex` and `view_as_real`. If these tensors however are named, this does not work, especially not when in 1.8 the previous fft is dropped. This is important in e.g. MRI reconstruction frameworks.

Supporting `view_as_complex` and `view_as_real` for named tensors would be useful too.

@zou3519 

cc @ezyang @anjali411 @dylanbespalko @mruberry @zou3519

## 🐛 Bug

Incorrect det value on CPU

## To Reproduce

```
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)

for N in [100,350,400,401]:
    W = torch.qr(torch.FloatTensor(N, N).normal_())[0]
    print('C = {}, det on cpu/gpu = {:.6f} / {:.6f}'.format(N,W.det(),W.cuda().det()))
```

```
C = 100, det on cpu/gpu = -0.999999 / -0.999999
C = 350, det on cpu/gpu = -173.111664 / -1.000001
```

stage1.title: forward AD inplace over view silently copies in some cases
stage1.body:
```
import torch
import torch.autograd.forward_ad as fwAD

base = torch.randn(2, 2)
view = base.transpose(0, 1)

primal = torch.randn(2, 2)
tangent = torch.randn(2, 2)

with fwAD.dual_level():
    dual = fwAD.make_dual(primal, tangent)
    view.mul_(dual)

    p, d = fwAD.unpack_dual(base)
    print(p, d)
    view *= 2
    p1, d1 = fwAD.unpack_dual(base)
    print(p1, d1)
```

Got:
```
tensor([[ 0.2850, -0.7018],
        [ 0.7845,  0.8536]]) tensor([[-0.0455,  0.6741],
        [-0.0869, -0.3255]])
tensor([[ 0.5701, -1.4037],
        [ 1.5691,  1.7072]]) tensor([[-0.0455,  0.6741],
        [-0.0869, -0.3255]])
```

Expected the tangent to also be doubled for the base.

This issue is that in the in-place over view case for forward AD, we only compare the layout of the new grad with the base. But in this case, due to the transpose, the layout of the base different from the view, so we end up creating a new copy later in _set_fw_grad.

This will no longer fail silently once I add the layout mismatch view assert.

cc @ezyang @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @pearu @nikitaved @soulitzer @Lezcano @Varal7

## 🐛 Bug

When using `torch.lstsq` to solve with specific values, `torch.lstsq` produces wrong result (on cuda) or raises error (on cpu) while `scipy.linalg.lstsq` not.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Use the dumped `.npy` file: `a.npy`, `b.npy` to perform `torch.lstsq`
2. Meanwhile, `lstsq` can also be solved in `scipy.linalg.lstsq`
3. With the given `numpy array`, `torch.lstsq` raises error on `cpu`, or gives wrong result on `cuda`, while `scipy.linalg.lstsq` not.

Code samples and error messages:

Download files:
* `a.npy`: https://github.com/xiaosu-zhu/archives/releases/download/torch.lstsq/a.npy
* `b.npy`: https://github.com/xiaosu-zhu/archives/releases/download/torch.lstsq/b.npy

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg
import torch

# sparse 0-1 matrix with shape [100000, 1024]
# each row contains exactly 4 ones and other zeros
a = np.load("a.npy").astype(np.float32)
# int matrix with shape [100000, 128]
b = np.load("b.npy").astype(np.float32)

x, _, _, _ = scipy.linalg.lstsq(a, b)

# 67480.16036171981
print(((a @ x - b) ** 2).sum(-1).mean())

b = torch.from_numpy(b).cuda()
a = torch.from_numpy(a).cuda()
x, _ = torch.lstsq(b, a)

# 7.4439e+15

# The 259-th diagonal element of the triangular factor of A is zero 
# at /opt/conda/conda-bld/pytorch_1595629395347/work/aten/src/TH/generic/THTensorLapack.cpp:177
x, _ = torch.lstsq(b.cpu(), a.cpu())
```

[mrshenli]: Hey @mruberry, do we also have plan to add a `lstsq` to `torch.linalg` and retire existing ones in the near future?

---

[mruberry]: Yes we do, see https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/42666. We would definitely take a fix for this.

---

[xiaosu-zhu]: Found related issue #11174

---

[chrisby]: In fact, I stumbled over the fact that you can reproduce this very easily with a 2 x 2 matrix:

```
from scipy import linalg
import torch

a = np.array([[0., 0.], [0., 1.]])
b = np.array([[0., 0.], [0., 1.]])

linalg.lstsq(a,b)[0] # Yields [[0., 0.], [0., 1.]]

a_t = torch.from_numpy(a)
b_t = torch.from_numpy(b)
torch.lstsq(a_t,b_t)
```
The last line throws `RuntimeError: Lapack Error in gels : The 1-th diagonal element of the triangular factor of A is zero at ../aten/src/TH/generic/THTensorLapack.cpp:177`

Is there a timeline on a fix? Seems to be rather relevant.

---

[mruberry]: Thanks for the simpler reproduction, @chrisby. 

Our team is currently working through linear algebra updates, but I've changed this issue to high priority. It should be fixed before the next release.

---

[xiaosu-zhu]: Thank you, @chrisby @mruberry. Look forward to the next release ❤️

---

[nikitaved]: The fix will probably require some thinking when it comes to handling rank-deficient inputs (which potentially leads to non-uniqueness). The current implementation is based on the LAPACK's [`?gels`](https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/documentation/mkl-developer-reference-fortran/top/lapack-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-driver-routines/linear-least-squares-lls-problems-lapack-driver-routines/gels.html),
and the documentation reads that it expects the input of full rank.

@mruberry , is someone working on this one already?

---

[mruberry]: @nikitaved To the best of my knowledge no one is working on this.

---

[xiaosu-zhu]: Yes, the current implementation can't handle rank-deficient matrices, while [`scipy.linalg.lstsq`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.lstsq.html) using three routines: [?gelss](https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/documentation/mkl-developer-reference-fortran/top/lapack-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-driver-routines/linear-least-squares-lls-problems-lapack-driver-routines/gelss.html), [?gelsd](https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/documentation/mkl-developer-reference-fortran/top/lapack-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-driver-routines/linear-least-squares-lls-problems-lapack-driver-routines/gelsd.html), [?gelsy](https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/documentation/mkl-developer-reference-fortran/top/lapack-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-routines/lapack-least-squares-and-eigenvalue-problem-driver-routines/linear-least-squares-lls-problems-lapack-driver-routines/gelsy.html), also from LAPACK.

---

[nikitaved]: `?gelss, ?gelsd, ?gelsy` use SVD, but handle rand-deficient cases, while `?gels` does not use SVD, hence is faster, but does not handle rank-deficient cases.
Does it make sense to entirely switch to the SVD solution in `torch.linalg.lstsq`? Yes, we loose some speed, but at least we can avoid nasty errors during long trainings if the input becomes rank-deficient.

---

[mruberry]: Generally we should bias towards numerical correctness/stability/precision. However, in this case we don't have to decide one or the other. We can add an optional parameter to `linalg.lstsq` to select the current faster but less stable option.

---

[chrisby]: Yeah, this is exactly how `scipy` is doing it:

```
if driver is None:
    driver = lstsq.default_lapack_driver
if driver not in ('gelsd', 'gelsy', 'gelss'):
    raise ValueError('LAPACK driver "%s" is not found' % driver)
```

---

[nikitaved]: Well, for CUDA it seems like Magma has only `?gels` that works only for overdetermined matrices. Fear not, we can still use SVD/pseudo inverse for underdetermined/rank-deficient inputs in CUDA.

---

[nikitaved]: @mruberry , I have started working on this issue. The next release you mentioned above is 1.7.1, right?

---

[mruberry]: 1.7.1 is only some bugfixes for the 1.7 release. The next release from nightly is 1.8.
