stage1.title: PyTorch 1.10.2 failed to create workable onnx for sequential LSTMs
stage1.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The following code export runnable onnx until PyTorch 1.10 (tested and still work in 1.8 & 1.9), the exported onnx no longer work after that.

```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class testModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(testModel, self).__init__()
        self.rnn1 = nn.LSTM(8, 8, bidirectional=True, batch_first=True)
        self.linear1 = nn.Linear(8 * 2, 8)

        self.rnn2 = nn.LSTM(8, 8, bidirectional=True, batch_first=True)
        self.linear2 = nn.Linear(8 * 2, 8)

    def forward(self, input):
        rnn_output1, _ = self.rnn1(input)
        linear_output1 = self.linear1(rnn_output1)

        rnn_output2, _ = self.rnn2(linear_output1)
        linear_output2 = self.linear2(rnn_output2)

        return linear_output2

net = testModel()
net.eval()
input = torch.zeros((1, 100, 8), dtype=torch.float32)

with torch.no_grad():
   output = net(input)


torch.onnx.export(
        net,
        input,
        'out.onnx',
        export_params=True,
        opset_version=13, 
        verbose=False,
        do_constant_folding=True,
        input_names = ['input'],
        output_names = ['output'],
        dynamic_axes={
                        'input' : {0 : 'batch_size',1:'w',2:'h'},
                        'output' : {0 : 'batch_size', 1:'w',2:'h'},
                }
        )

##### ONNXRuntime ####
import onnxruntime as rt
import numpy as np
sess = rt.InferenceSession('out.onnx')
result_1 = sess.run([], {'input': input.numpy()})[0] # Failed
``` 

Error Message from onnxruntime
```
[E:onnxruntime:, sequential_executor.cc:346 Execute] Non-zero status code returned while running LSTM node. Name:'LSTM_38' Status Message: Input initial_h must have shape {2,1,8}. Actual:{2,0,8}
```

After inspect the model with Netron, it seem like PyTorch produce invalid expand layers in the circle
![out onnx-2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/987946/152692491-53f33d84-7d53-45e1-af18-0ca7d8edfb3a.png)

Workable onnx graph from PyTorch 1.9.0 (generated from above code)
![out onnx-3](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/987946/152693371-fefce667-eefe-4b00-969b-9e0c0ca347f3.png)

### Versions

pytorch 1.10.2
onnxruntime 1.10
onnx 1.10.2

cc @malfet @albanD

stage1.title: Implementation of 2d bicubic grid sampler
stage1.body:
## 🚀 Feature
support 2d bicubic interpolation in `nn.function.grid_sample` in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/25039

## Pitch

Using the [2d bicubic convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicubic_interpolation) just as `torch.nn.functional.interpolate()` [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/UpSampleBicubic2d.cpp).

## Additional context
I would like to implement this feature, and there are some questions
1. There are two cpu code about the grid_sample, `aten/src/Aten/native/GridSampler.cpp` and `aten/src/Aten/native/cpu/GridSamplerKernel.cpp`, and also the dispatch mechanism in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a309355be3d2c12dfdca17ee34a8259654c5b823/aten/src/ATen/native/GridSampler.cpp#L640
Are there any concern or recommend about the priority? I think I should first implement in `aten/src/Aten/native/GridSampler.cpp` and `aten/src/Aten/native/cuda/GridSampler.cu`. If success, try to implement in `aten/src/Aten/native/cpu/GridSamplerKernel.cpp` for AVX2

2. How could I test my implementation? There is `remap` function in openCV to test the forward correctness, but how about the backward? Use existed bicubic upsampling could cover some cases, but not general. Any suggestions would be appreciated

Thanks

cc @albanD @mruberry

stage1.title: COO to CSR tensor conversion is slow
stage1.body:
Originally raised in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/50937#discussion_r604346660

The COO to CSR tensor conversion is implemented in
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/3a777b67926c5f02bc287b25e572c521d6d11fb0/torch/_tensor.py#L928-L940
and it consists of two time-consuming parts:
- coalescing if the COO tensor is uncoaleasced
- row indices compression procedure

Indeed, taking a coalesced COO sample with `size=(1000, 1000)` and `nnz=500`, about 1.5% of the `to_sparse_csr` call time is spend in coalescing and 98% of the time in running the row indices compression loop.

The slowness of the row indices compression loop has two origins:
- it is implemented in Python
- it uses a suboptimal algorithm

Indeed, a sample of row indices with `size[0] == 1000` and `nnz=500`, a pure Python algorithm in
https://github.com/pearu/gcs/blob/b54ba0cba9c853b797274ef26b6c42386f2cafa3/gcs/storage.py#L24-L45
is about 3x faster than used in `to_sparse_csr`, and when applying `numba.njit` to the `compress_indices` function, about 83x speedup is achieved compared to `to_sparse_csr`.

The performance of COO to CSR tensor conversion can be improved by implementing a more efficient row indices compression algorithm (see `compress_indices` referenced above) in C++.

cc @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel @aocsa @nikitaved @pearu @mruberry

stage3_gold.comments:
[ngimel]: How about using `torch.searchsorted` for this?

---

[pearu]: Use unsafe CSR constructor when it becomes available: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/57274#discussion_r629580597

---

[pearu]: xref: [..conversion from COO to CSR is ridiculously slow on CUDA device.](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/16187#issuecomment-869735963)

---

[pearu]: Since CSR `crow_indices` are always 1D, use `torch.bucketize` instead of `torch.searchsorted` for efficiency.

---

[cpuhrsch]: cc @rusty1s

---

[rusty1s]: I've done some benchmarking efforts and pushed them to the `torch-sparse` package, see [here](https://github.com/rusty1s/pytorch_sparse/blob/master/benchmark/ptr2ind.py).

I compared the current PyTorch implementation, the `compress_indices` implementation, a vectorized version using `bincount` and `cumsum`, and the dedicated implementation sitting in [`torch-sparse`](https://github.com/rusty1s/pytorch_sparse/blob/master/csrc/cpu/convert_cpu.cpp#L7-L35), using real-world sparse matrices:

---

[pearu]: @rusty1s thanks for the benchmarks! A couple of notes. The benchmarks compare pure single-thread Python and parallel C++ implementations and the `1 000..10 000`-fold difference is not surprising.

If possible, could you also benchmark
- the different algorithms under the same implementation environment, that is, all in C++ using parallel_for
- using searchsorted/bucketize approach that could provide immediate CUDA backend support to COO->CSR conversion

---

[rusty1s]: The `torch-sparse` C++ implementation already implements the `compress_indices` algorithms mentioned above. For the current COO2CSR PyTorch implementation, I don't think it's possible to make use of multi-threading at all.

I also updated the benchmark script to support both `searchsorted`/`bucketize` functions:
```

========================================================

bucketize:    0.004996270923824101

searchsorted: 0.0050520981201017745
bucketize:    0.00515870925077458

StocF-1465.mat: shape=(1465137, 1465137) nnz=21005389
=====================================================
torch-sparse: 0.011693406884915361
searchsorted: 0.03374433517456055
bucketize:    0.032992157496904075

ldoor.mat: shape=(952203, 952203) nnz=42493817
==============================================
torch-sparse: 0.017606527872488533
searchsorted: 0.030941883722941082
bucketize:    0.02959784530323638
```
Both are about 3 times slower than the current `torch-sparse` function (probably because of the extra `torch.arange` call?).

---

[pearu]: It sounds like torch-sparse C++/parallel_for implementation of the coo->csr operation is a way to go for CPU. Notice that this implementation needs a specialization for int64-COO -> int32-CSR because, in PyTorch, COO tensors use int64 indices while CSR tensors use int32 indices (because PyTorch is tied to LP64 MKL, and on CPU, MKL sparse tools are used for computations).
 
For indices stored on CUDA device, multiple choices are possible:
1. implement torch-sparse/compress_indices algorithm for CUDA
2. use bucketize for CUDA as a first instance when 1. is not available
3. copy indices to CPU, perform coo->csr operation using CPU method, copy crow_indices to CUDA as a first instance when 1. is not available.
4. anything else?

@rusty1s , what do you think?

---

[rusty1s]: I‘m in favor of option (1) or (2), and will work on that with @cpuhrsch.

---

[ngimel]: >For the current COO2CSR PyTorch implementation, I don't think it's possible to make use of multi-threading at all.

searchsorted/bucketize are dispatched to the same implementation, so it's not surprising that they produce similar results.
searchsorted/bucketize uses multithreading - it's doing independent binary searches for each element. Overhead from `arange` should be minimal (can be confirmed), so maybe the best thing is to add sequential implementation to searchsorted, so that all searchsorted usecases can benefit too, not just coo2csr?

model_evidence.title: COO to CSR tensor conversion is slow
model_evidence.body:
Originally raised in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/50937#discussion_r604346660

The COO to CSR tensor conversion is implemented in
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/3a777b67926c5f02bc287b25e572c521d6d11fb0/torch/_tensor.py#L928-L940
and it consists of two time-consuming parts:
- coalescing if the COO tensor is uncoaleasced
- row indices compression procedure

Indeed, taking a coalesced COO sample with `size=(1000, 1000)` and `nnz=500`, about 1.5% of the `to_sparse_csr` call time is spend in coalescing and 98% of the time in running the row indices compression loop.

The slowness of the row indices compression loop has two origins:
- it is implemented in Python
- it uses a suboptimal algorithm

Indeed, a sample of row indices with `size[0] == 1000` and `nnz=500`, a pure Python algorithm in
https://github.com/pearu/gcs/blob/b54ba0cba9c853b797274ef26b6c42386f2cafa3/gcs/storage.py#L24-L45
is about 3x faster than used in `to_sparse_csr`, and when applying `numba.njit` to the `compress_indices` function, about 83x speedup is achieved compared to `to_sparse_csr`.

The performance of COO to CSR tensor conversion can be improved by implementing a more efficient row indices compression algorithm (see `compress_indices` referenced above) in C++.

cc @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel @aocsa @nikitaved @pearu @mruberry

stage1.title: Lint rule that checks that new test files are being tested in CI
stage1.body:
## 🚀 Feature
We should have a lint rule that checks that new python test files are being tested in CI (i.e. are added to run_test.py)

## Motivation

It's really easy to forget to add a test to run_test.py. In particular, I noticed recently that we're missing `test/test_python_dispatch.py` from `run_test.py`.

## Pitch

Add some lint rule. Upon creation of a new `test_*.py` file under the `test/` folder, check that the file also gets added to a list in `run_test.py`.

## Alternatives

Better documentation around what to do when you're adding a new test file?

cc @ezyang @seemethere @malfet @walterddr @lg20987 @pytorch/pytorch-dev-infra @mruberry @VitalyFedyunin

```python
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = 6.
size = 10. ** 6

x = torch.rand((1,int(size),poolsize), requires_grad=True).to('cuda:0')
y = F.max_pool1d(x.contiguous(), kernel_size=poolsize, stride=None, padding=0)

loss = torch.sum(y)
```

As a temporary solution, we added `worker_name_to_id` to the rpc init API to simplify RpcAgent initialization process. Ideally, each RpcAgent implementation should either communicate directly to collect all names or read the names from the store (initialized by using the `init_method` arg). Bottom line is that `worker_name_to_id` should not appear in the final API.

```
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F

A = torch.ones(2)
```

stage1.title: Different speed between BatchNorm1d and BatchNorm2d
stage1.body:
Hi I assume BatchNorm1d and BatchNorm2d (or 3d) should have same performance. However when normalizing a tensor of shape `(L, C) = (B*H*W, C)` by BatchNorm1d, the speed is >5x slower than BatchNorm2d on a shape of `(B, C, H, W)`. Is this expected or is there a way to speed up?

Reproducer:

```
import torch

def time_bn(bn, x):
    start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    start.record()
    x = bn(x)
    end.record()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(start.elapsed_time(end))
    return x

shape = (50, 50, 50, 50)
a = torch.rand(shape)
b = a.flatten(0, -2)

bna = torch.nn.BatchNorm2d(50)
bnb = torch.nn.BatchNorm1d(50)

time_bn(bna, a)
time_bn(bnb, b)
```

Output:
```
11.409407615661621
89.55596923828125
```

## Environment

```
 - PyTorch Version: tested on 1.4/1.5
 - OS: Ubuntu 18.04
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): conda
 - Python version: 3.7/3.8
 - CUDA/cuDNN version: 10.1
 - GPU models and configuration: GTX 1070
 - Any other relevant information:
```

---

---

[ngimel]: The sizes in the issue are particularly bad for our BatchNorm1d implementation (large batch, 125000, and small number of features, 50). While it's possible to have an implementation that does well on these sizes (and e.g. our regular reduction kernels mostly do well in this case), BatchNorm1d was not optimized for this usecase. Is it common?

---

[vadimkantorov]: (Maybe this is somehow related: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/37713)

---

[mruberry]: Lowering priority. We're not sure how natural this example is.

---

[vadimkantorov]: IIUC LxC example is very natural, it's audio and other long-time, few-channels signals

---

[rusty1s]: I and other users of PyTorch Geometric recently noticed the runtime issues with `torch.nn.BatchNorm1d` as well (https://github.com/rusty1s/pytorch_geometric/issues/2394). I personally always wondered why applying batch normalization in Graph Neural Networks make things so slow.

In GNNs, we do not have a "batch" dimension but rather want to normalize across the node dimension within a node feature matrix of shape `[num_nodes, num_features]`. In general, `num_nodes >> num_features`. Manually implementing a `BatchNorm` module for this specific use-case can be up to 15 times faster than using regular `torch.nn.BatchNorm1d`.

Given the popularity of implementing GNNs in PyTorch, I would be very happy to see this addressed :)

model_evidence.title: Different speed between BatchNorm1d and BatchNorm2d
model_evidence.body:
Hi I assume BatchNorm1d and BatchNorm2d (or 3d) should have same performance. However when normalizing a tensor of shape `(L, C) = (B*H*W, C)` by BatchNorm1d, the speed is >5x slower than BatchNorm2d on a shape of `(B, C, H, W)`. Is this expected or is there a way to speed up?

Reproducer:

```
import torch

def time_bn(bn, x):
    start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    start.record()
    x = bn(x)
    end.record()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(start.elapsed_time(end))
    return x

shape = (50, 50, 50, 50)
a = torch.rand(shape)
b = a.flatten(0, -2)

bna = torch.nn.BatchNorm2d(50)
bnb = torch.nn.BatchNorm1d(50)

time_bn(bna, a)
time_bn(bnb, b)
```

Output:
```
11.409407615661621
89.55596923828125
```

## Environment

```
 - PyTorch Version: tested on 1.4/1.5
 - OS: Ubuntu 18.04
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): conda
 - Python version: 3.7/3.8
 - CUDA/cuDNN version: 10.1
 - GPU models and configuration: GTX 1070
 - Any other relevant information:
```

stage1.title: LNK2019 error when linking onnx_torch on Windows with BUILD_TEST=0
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

When building PyTorch from source on Windows, there are multiple `LNK2019 unresolved external symbol` errors when trying to link classes in the onnx_torch:: namespace.

I've found this problem when building from source on different Windows machines, and using different build flags. But it always happens when using `BUILD_TEST=0`, and it doesn't happen when `BUILD_TEST=1`.

This has been reported before by @realiti4 :
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/45060#issuecomment-698519994

And a workaround has been suggested by @droberts195 :
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/45060#issuecomment-766332179
https://github.com/elastic/ml-cpp/pull/1692/files#r563279574

But I'm opening this issue since those comments appear on a closed issue.

By using the workaround by @droberts195 my build seems to be successful even when using `BUILD_TEST=0`, although I haven't run any tests with that build to verify it's all correct. The workaround is simply to move the` list(APPEND ...)` outside of the `if(BUILD_TEST) `block:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/1f40f2a1723fd3b9302bea3829f2570c8e0e7e94/torch/CMakeLists.txt#L98-L100

Why is it inside the `if(BUILD_TEST)` block, i.e. why is the `onnx_library` only linked on windows when `BUILD_TEST=1`? Perhaps to solve this bug it's simply a matter to modify that block, and always link the `onnx_library` even when `BUILD_TEST=0`?

## To Reproduce
1. set BUILD_TEST=0
2. python setup.py develop

## Expected behavior
For the build to succeed even with `BUILD_TEST=0` on Windows

model_evidence.title: LNK2019 error when linking onnx_torch on Windows with BUILD_TEST=0
model_evidence.body:
## 🐛 Bug

When building PyTorch from source on Windows, there are multiple `LNK2019 unresolved external symbol` errors when trying to link classes in the onnx_torch:: namespace.

I've found this problem when building from source on different Windows machines, and using different build flags. But it always happens when using `BUILD_TEST=0`, and it doesn't happen when `BUILD_TEST=1`.

This has been reported before by @realiti4 :
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/45060#issuecomment-698519994

And a workaround has been suggested by @droberts195 :
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/45060#issuecomment-766332179
https://github.com/elastic/ml-cpp/pull/1692/files#r563279574

But I'm opening this issue since those comments appear on a closed issue.

By using the workaround by @droberts195 my build seems to be successful even when using `BUILD_TEST=0`, although I haven't run any tests with that build to verify it's all correct. The workaround is simply to move the` list(APPEND ...)` outside of the `if(BUILD_TEST) `block:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/1f40f2a1723fd3b9302bea3829f2570c8e0e7e94/torch/CMakeLists.txt#L98-L100

Why is it inside the `if(BUILD_TEST)` block, i.e. why is the `onnx_library` only linked on windows when `BUILD_TEST=1`? Perhaps to solve this bug it's simply a matter to modify that block, and always link the `onnx_library` even when `BUILD_TEST=0`?

## To Reproduce
1. set BUILD_TEST=0
2. python setup.py develop

## Expected behavior
For the build to succeed even with `BUILD_TEST=0` on Windows

## Additional context
Error log with CMAKE_VERBOSE_MAKEFILE=1:

stage1.title: torch.normal only issues error for negative sigma when shape argument is given
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

As explained in [this forum thread](https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/how-does-torch-normal-work-with-a-negative-standard-deviation/107571/3) torch.normal only gives an error for negative sigma when there is no size argument given in. Code examples are below.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

This code cause an error...

```
torch.manual_seed(8)
torch.normal(0, -1, (10, ))

# output
# RuntimeError                              Traceback (most recent call last)
# <ipython-input-6-f3bb1e6c1119> in <module>()
    #   1 torch.manual_seed(8)
# ----> 2 torch.normal(0, -1, (10, ))

# RuntimeError: normal_ expects std > 0.0, but found std=-1
```

while this code causes no error...

```
mu = torch.tensor(0.0)
sigma = torch.tensor(-3.0)
torch.normal(mu, sigma)

# ...output
>>> torch.normal(mu, sigma)
tensor(-3.6977)
>>> torch.normal(mu, sigma)
tensor(-3.0448)
>>> torch.normal(mu, sigma)
tensor(-0.2327)
```

<!-- If you have a code sample, error messages, stack traces, please provide it here as well -->

## Expected behavior

I would expect that the error reporting would be consistent and that a negative standard deviation on a singleton sample would also give an error.

stage3_gold.comments:
[ngimel]: Thanks for reporting, it's a bug. The problematic functions are here https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e44b2b72bd4ccecf9c2f6c18d09c11eff446b5a3/aten/src/ATen/native/DistributionTemplates.h#L219-L249, they don't check that std is positive. 
High pri for silent correctness, however, checking if std is valid is a perf penalty, we should discuss if we want it.

---

[jeffwillette]: As I said in the forum thread I came across this bug in a repository where the user had no positive condition such as training the parameter in the log-space or using a softplus. I was confused as to why their code was working and more confused when I saw no error in Pytorch. 

I would strongly side in favor of checking even if there is a performance penalty because it is:

- very confusing that it fails only with the size argument
- silently works even though the user may be totally wrong in the way that they call it.

---

[mruberry]: We would accept a PR fixing this on CPU. We're OK with checking the values of the tensor and paying the performance penalty on CPU. We should document this is validated on CPU but not on CUDA. 

Note for the future: it would be interesting to investigate adding a CUDA assert for CUDA.

---

[gchanan]: @ngimel argued we can't (easily) on-device assert TensorIterator because our lambdas aren't complicated/smart enough.  It would be good to figure out how difficult it would be to do this.

---

[jeffwillette]: I do not think it would be a good idea to add another inconsistent behavior on top of an existing one. If it can't be synced across CPU/CUDA. Would it be better to just document that a single sample (without size arg) does not enforce a positive sigma constraint?

---

[fritzo]: (removing `module: distributions` label because the `distributions.Normal` wrapper already checks for negative sigma)

---

[ousou]: I noticed that the same error is present in PyTorch version 1.7.1 also when using the distributions.Normal wrapper. This makes the log_prob function return NaN on any value:

```
>>> a = torch.distributions.Normal(0,-1)
>>> a.log_prob(0)
tensor(nan)
>>> a.log_prob(1)
tensor(nan)
>>> a.log_prob(0.5)
tensor(nan)
>>> a.log_prob(-0.5)
tensor(nan)
```

---

[kshitij12345]: @ousou Looks to be fixed in master. Can you try nightly

```python
>>> a = torch.distributions.Normal(0,-1)
ValueError: The parameter scale has invalid values
```

---

[kurtamohler]: This issue was fixed by #51317, apparently I didn't link it to auto close.

---

[pjh4993]: I found that during training model, gradient can change sigma to negative
Is that not bug and responsibility to check for negative sigma is for user?

---

[kurtamohler]: If the gradient calculation is changing sigma, that seems like an issue. The backward functions for `torch.normal` should only be setting gradients to zero, so sigma (called `std` here) shouldn't change: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/056a8e0d5cc6b53dd574b77eebf273ded646f81e/tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml#L1051-L1062

Do you have a reproducer script @pjh4993?

---

[jkbh]: I was wondering why the behaviour was changed from requiring std < 0 to std <= 0. The normal distrbution is not defined for std=0 and I think this can still lead to silent correctness and unexpectedly working code.

---

[kurtamohler]: @jkbh, I'm not a math expert by any means, so I don't know any of the formalism behind this. But as the standard deviation of a normal distribution approaches 0, the range of possible outputs shrinks to include only the mean of the distribution. Numpy does this as well:

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import torch
>>> np.random.normal(loc=1, scale=0, size=())
array(1.)
>>> torch.normal(mean=1, std=0, size=())
tensor(1.)
```

Maybe someone else here can give a more rigorous explanation than me

stage1.title: [FR] More consistent matrix norm for torch.norm
stage1.body:
`torch.norm` currently have the following inconsistent behavior where for matrix inputs and `ord` is a numerical value, **vector** norm is computed instead:
```
            =====  ============================  ==========================
            ord    matrix norm                   vector norm
            =====  ============================  ==========================
            None   Frobenius norm                2-norm
            'fro'  Frobenius norm                --
            'nuc'  nuclear norm                  --
            Other  as vec norm when dim is None  sum(abs(x)**ord)**(1./ord)
            =====  ============================  ==========================
```
(Even though the last row reads `when dim is None`, same behavior happens when `dim` is a 2-tuple).


However, the matrix Lpq norms are useful. And users are justified in expecting that `mat.norm(2)` computes the L2 norm (max e-value) since `mat.norm('fro')` computes the matrix Frobenius norm. If we follow the [NumPy interface](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.norm.html), the following behavior should be less surprising and error prune:

```

    =====  ============================  ==========================
    ord    norm for matrices             norm for vectors
    =====  ============================  ==========================
    None   Frobenius norm                2-norm
    'fro'  Frobenius norm                --
    'nuc'  nuclear norm                  --
    inf    max(sum(abs(x), axis=1))      max(abs(x))
    -inf   min(sum(abs(x), axis=1))      min(abs(x))
    0      --                            sum(x != 0)
    1      max(sum(abs(x), axis=0))      as below
    -1     min(sum(abs(x), axis=0))      as below
    2      2-norm (largest sing. value)  as below
    -2     smallest singular value       as below
    other  --                            sum(abs(x)**ord)**(1./ord)
    =====  ============================  ==========================
```

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @SsnL @vishwakftw @jianyuh

stage3_gold.comments:
[vadimkantorov]: Related about the spectral matrix norm: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/12760

---

[vishwakftw]: How does NumPy handle batching?

For instance, a 4 x 3 matrix can also be interpreted as 4 size-3 vectors.

---

[vishwakftw]: So, I did some trials and this is what I found:
- If inputs are 2-D and axis is not specified, then the input is considered to be a matrix
- If inputs are 2-D and an axis is specified, then the input is considered to be a batch of vectors whose corresponding norms are output
- If inputs are > 2-D, then an axis argument is mandatory when `ord` is not `None`. Furthermore, you will have to provide one axis for vector inputs, and 2 axes for matrix inputs.

---

[ezyang]: It does seem like this may merit a BC-breaking change. Some things we should check before doing so: (1) when was this consistency introduced, (2) is the inconsistent behavior tested for in our test suite, or is this actually totally untested.

This seems like a case where we can easily give a deprecation warning, since the forward compatible way of batching (specify an axis explicitly) works today,

---

[VitalyFedyunin]: We need to separate 'needs discussion' label from the triage process.

---

[ailzhang]: ~Any objections if we fix the documentation first for 1.3? Now it says we give matrix norm in some cases, which is not true.~
[Edit: ] Nvm the documentation matches our behavior which "redefines" matrices norm to be same as vec norm for non-fro and non-nuc norms. https://pytorch.org/docs/master/torch.html#torch.norm 
I'd strong prefer a BC breaking change. Assigning myself for now, will try to find some time to fix later if no one beats me to it.

---

[kurtamohler]: @ailzhang , are you still planning on doing this? If not, I would be happy to take over.

---

[ailzhang]: Hey @kurtamohler , feel free to take it over! Please let us know if you need any help! Thanks!

---

[kurtamohler]: Cool, thanks!

---

[kurtamohler]: I don't fully understand what numpy's norm is supposed to do when `ord=2` in the matrix norm case. The documentation says `2-norm (largest sing. value)`, which is unclear to me. "largest sing. value" would seem to just mean `max(x, axis=(0,1))`, but that's not the result I get:
```
>>> numpy.linalg.norm(numpy.array([[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]), ord=2, axis=(0,1))
9.50803200069572
```

---

[vishwakftw]: Largest singular value is the largest value of the diagonal elements of S, where X = USV^{T} (SVD).

---

[kurtamohler]: Got it, thanks @vishwakftw!

```
def approx_spectral_largest(a, iters: int, method: str):
    class MyModule(torch.nn.Module):
        def __init__(self, weight):
            super(MyModule, self).__init__()
            self.weight = torch.nn.Parameter(weight)
    
        def forward(self):
            return self.weight
    
    b = torch.nn.utils.spectral_norm(
        MyModule(a),
        n_power_iterations=iters)()
    
    if method == 'median':
        return (a / b).median()
    elif method == 'mean':
        return (a / b).mean()
    else:
        raise RuntimeError('method "%s" not available' % method)
```

model_evidence.title: [FR] More consistent matrix norm for torch.norm
model_evidence.body:
`torch.norm` currently have the following inconsistent behavior where for matrix inputs and `ord` is a numerical value, **vector** norm is computed instead:
```
            =====  ============================  ==========================
            ord    matrix norm                   vector norm
            =====  ============================  ==========================
            None   Frobenius norm                2-norm
            'fro'  Frobenius norm                --
            'nuc'  nuclear norm                  --
            Other  as vec norm when dim is None  sum(abs(x)**ord)**(1./ord)
            =====  ============================  ==========================
```
(Even though the last row reads `when dim is None`, same behavior happens when `dim` is a 2-tuple).


However, the matrix Lpq norms are useful. And users are justified in expecting that `mat.norm(2)` computes the L2 norm (max e-value) since `mat.norm('fro')` computes the matrix Frobenius norm. If we follow the [NumPy interface](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.norm.html), the following behavior should be less surprising and error prune:

```

    =====  ============================  ==========================
    ord    norm for matrices             norm for vectors
    =====  ============================  ==========================
    None   Frobenius norm                2-norm
    'fro'  Frobenius norm                --
    'nuc'  nuclear norm                  --
    inf    max(sum(abs(x), axis=1))      max(abs(x))
    -inf   min(sum(abs(x), axis=1))      min(abs(x))
    0      --                            sum(x != 0)
    1      max(sum(abs(x), axis=0))      as below
    -1     min(sum(abs(x), axis=0))      as below
    2      2-norm (largest sing. value)  as below
    -2     smallest singular value       as below
    other  --                            sum(abs(x)**ord)**(1./ord)
    =====  ============================  ==========================
```

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @SsnL @vishwakftw @jianyuh

SyncBatchNorm layers in torch 1.10.0 give different outputs on 2 gpus vs the equivalent BatchNorm layer on a single gpu. This wasn't a problem in torch 1.8.0

## To Reproduce
This code is based on the [PyTorch DDP demo](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/ddp_tutorial.html) but the model consists only of a `BatchNorm2d` layer.

```python
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.multiprocessing as mp

from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
import argparse


def setup(rank, world_size):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "localhost"
    os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = "12355"

    # iniialize the process group
    dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)


def cleanup():
    dist.destroy_process_group()


class ToyModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_features=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(num_features=num_features)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        x = self.bn(x)
        x = x.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        return x


def demo_basic(rank, world_size, convert_sync_batchnorm):
    print(f"Running basic DDP example on rank {rank}.")
    setup(rank, world_size)

    # create model and move it to GPU with id rank
    model = ToyModel(num_features=10)
    # create model and move it to GPU with id rank
    if world_size > 1 and convert_sync_batchnorm:
        print("Converting BatchNorm to SyncBatchNorm")
        model = torch.nn.SyncBatchNorm.convert_sync_batchnorm(model)

    model = model.to(rank)
    if world_size > 1:
        ddp_model = DDP(model, device_ids=[rank])
        model = ddp_model

    inputs = torch.randn(2, 2, 10, 1).to(rank)
    print(f"{rank=}, {inputs[0, 0].squeeze()=}")

    print(f"{rank=}, {outputs[0, 0].squeeze()=}")

    parser.add_argument("--n_gpus", default=2, type=int, help="Number of gpus")
    parser.add_argument(
```

```python 
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.multiprocessing as mp

from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
import argparse


def setup(rank, world_size):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "localhost"
    os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = "12355"

    # iniialize the process group
    dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)


def cleanup():
    dist.destroy_process_group()


class ToyModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_features=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(num_features=num_features)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.bn(x)
        return x


def demo_basic(rank, world_size, convert_sync_batchnorm, permute):
    print(f"Running basic DDP example on rank {rank}.")
    setup(rank, world_size)

    # create model and move it to GPU with id rank
    model = ToyModel(num_features=3)
    # create model and move it to GPU with id rank
    if world_size > 1 and convert_sync_batchnorm:
        print("Converting BatchNorm to SyncBatchNorm")
        model = torch.nn.SyncBatchNorm.convert_sync_batchnorm(model)

    model = model.to(rank)
    if world_size > 1:
        ddp_model = DDP(model, device_ids=[rank])
        model = ddp_model

    inputs = torch.randn(2, 3, 3, 1).to(rank)
    if permute:
        inputs = inputs.permute(0,2,1,3)
    print(f"{rank=}, {inputs[0].squeeze()=}")
    outputs = model(inputs)
    print(f"{rank=}, {outputs.squeeze()=}")

    cleanup()


def run_demo(demo_fn, world_size, convert_bn, permute):
    if world_size > 1:
        mp.spawn(demo_fn, args=(world_size, convert_bn, permute), nprocs=world_size, join=True)
    else:
        demo_fn(0, world_size, convert_bn, permute)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--n_gpus", default=2, type=int, help="Number of gpus")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--convert_bn",
        action="store_true",
        default=False,
        help="Whether to convert BatchNorm layers to SyncBatchNorm",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--permute",
        action="store_true",
        default=False,
        help="Whether to convert BatchNorm layers to SyncBatchNorm",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    print(f"{torch.__version__=}")
    run_demo(demo_basic, args.n_gpus, args.convert_bn, args.permute)
```

[erees1]: Thanks for the reply @ngimel - I have rebuilt off the latest commit 1.10.0a0+git3df4870 and am finding the discrepancy from this example has been fixed. I am still doing some digging as I am finding using `SyncBatchNorm` vs `BatchNorm2D` slightly degrades the performance of our models wheras in in torch 1.8.0 it slightly improved performance (same data, same models).

---

[ngimel]: cc @peterbell10. Implementation of syncBatchNorm was slightly changed in 1.9 as a part of generally improving speed of BatchNorm1d that shares the same kernels, but the difference should be within fp limits. If you have data to suggest otherwise, please share.

---

[peterbell10]: I have confirmed this is fixed in master, and that #62839 specifically was the fix.

The issue is that the input tensor has `shape=[2, 10, 2, 1]` and `strides=[20, 1, 10, 1]`. This doesn't strictly have the strides of a channels-last tensor (because of the last dimension) and so `suggest_memory_format` returns contiguous and a contiguous output is allocated. However,  `is_contiguous(MemoryFormat::ChannelsLast)` which is used to select the implementation did accept the tensor because it ignores the strides of length-1 dimensions. The end result is the channels last kernel being called with an NHCW contiguous output and so it's assuming the wrong strides.

So, the correctness bug is fixed but it's now using the slower generic kernel. I'll work on a PR to fix that.

model_evidence.title: BatchNorm2d + SyncBatchNorm incorrect multi gpu behaviour in 1.10.0 (tested working in 1.8.0)
model_evidence.body:
## 🐛 Bug

SyncBatchNorm layers in torch 1.10.0 give different outputs on 2 gpus vs the equivalent BatchNorm layer on a single gpu. This wasn't a problem in torch 1.8.0

## To Reproduce
This code is based on the [PyTorch DDP demo](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/ddp_tutorial.html) but the model consists only of a `BatchNorm2d` layer.

```python
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.multiprocessing as mp

from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
import argparse


def setup(rank, world_size):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "localhost"
    os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = "12355"

    # iniialize the process group
    dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)


def cleanup():
    dist.destroy_process_group()


class ToyModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_features=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(num_features=num_features)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        x = self.bn(x)
        x = x.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)
        return x


def demo_basic(rank, world_size, convert_sync_batchnorm):
    print(f"Running basic DDP example on rank {rank}.")
    setup(rank, world_size)

    # create model and move it to GPU with id rank
    model = ToyModel(num_features=10)
    # create model and move it to GPU with id rank
    if world_size > 1 and convert_sync_batchnorm:
        print("Converting BatchNorm to SyncBatchNorm")
        model = torch.nn.SyncBatchNorm.convert_sync_batchnorm(model)

    model = model.to(rank)
    if world_size > 1:
        ddp_model = DDP(model, device_ids=[rank])
        model = ddp_model

    inputs = torch.randn(2, 2, 10, 1).to(rank)
    print(f"{rank=}, {inputs[0, 0].squeeze()=}")
    outputs = model(inputs)
    print(f"{rank=}, {outputs[0, 0].squeeze()=}")

    cleanup()


def run_demo(demo_fn, world_size, convert_bn):
    if world_size > 1:
        mp.spawn(demo_fn, args=(world_size, convert_bn), nprocs=world_size, join=True)
    else:
        demo_fn(0, world_size, convert_bn)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--n_gpus", default=2, type=int, help="Number of gpus")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--convert_bn",
        action="store_true",
        default=False,
        help="Whether to convert BatchNorm layers to SyncBatchNorm",
    )

    args = parser.parse_args()

    print(f"{torch.__version__=}")
    run_demo(demo_basic, args.n_gpus, args.convert_bn)
```

stage1.title: RuntimeError: ONNX export failed: Couldn't export operator aten::one_hot
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

Export of `F.one_hot` to ONNX format fails.

## To Reproduce
```
class TestMod(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, size, maxint=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.maxint = maxint
        self.weight = torch.randint(0, maxint, [size])

    def forward(self, x):
        return F.one_hot(self.weight, num_classes=self.maxint)
test = TestMod(3)
torch.onnx.export(test, test.weight, "test.onnx", verbose=True)
```

```cmake
    COMMAND "${PYTHON_EXECUTABLE}" -c
    "import hashlib;hash=hashlib.sha256();hash.update(open('${CUDA_NVRTC_LIB}','rb').read());print(hash.hexdigest()[:8])"
    RESULT_VARIABLE _retval
    OUTPUT_VARIABLE CUDA_NVRTC_SHORTHASH)

    message(WARNING "Failed to compute shorthash for libnvrtc.so")
    set(CUDA_NVRTC_SHORTHASH "XXXXXXXX")
```

Which mean that the python script: `"import hashlib;hash=hashlib.sha256();hash.update(open('${CUDA_NVRTC_LIB}','rb').read());print(hash.hexdigest()[:8])"` had failed.

```bash

```

And then rerun the python script above and it seems to work with an output like this:
```console
703109d3
```

But the problem `Failed to compute shorthash for libnvrtc.so` still persist when I run cmake build

stage1.title: Numerical instability in DivBackward0 for multiple backward
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

A simple division operation: `g = x/y` could produce numerical instability if multiple backward is applied.
This is because the derivative is calculated by `-grad * self / (other * other)` (see `tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml` in `div.Tensor`).
The `other` tensor is squared in one backward operation, so multiple operation will raise `other` to the power of `2^n` and can reach `inf` or `0` very quickly.
A simple fix should be sufficient: by replacing the derivative calculation to `-grad * result / other`, but it makes a bunch of tests fail (I'm not sure why).

## To see the problem

    import torch

    class Div2(torch.autograd.Function):
        @staticmethod
        def forward(ctx, x, y):
            z = x / y
            ctx.save_for_backward(x, y, z)
            return z

        @staticmethod
        def backward(ctx, gz):
            x, y, z = ctx.saved_tensors
            gx = Div2.apply(gz, y)
            gy = Div2.apply(-gz*z, y)
            return gx, gy

    def example(g, y, n):
        gs = [g.item()]
        for i in range(n):
            g, = torch.autograd.grad(g, (y,), create_graph=True)
            gs.append(g.item())
        return gs

    if __name__ == "__main__":
        a = 1e-8
        x = torch.tensor(a, requires_grad=True)
        y = torch.tensor(a, requires_grad=True)
        n = 4
        factorial = lambda i: 1 if i < 2 else i * factorial(i-1)
        print("Div1 (current implementation):")
        print(example(x / y, y, n))
        print("Div2 (proposed implementation):")
        print(example(Div2.apply(x, y), y, n))
        print("Actual:")
        actual = [(-1)**i*factorial(i)/(a**i) for i in range(n+1)] # [1.0, -1/a, 2/(a*a), -3*2/(a*a*a), 4*3*2/(a**4)]
        print(actual)

Output: 

    Div1 (current implementation):
    [1.0, -100000000.0, 1.99999983976448e+16, -inf, nan]
    Div2 (proposed implementation):
    [1.0, -100000000.0, 2.000000054512845e+16, -6.000000083090567e+24, 2.4000002343777533e+33]
    Actual:
    [1.0, -100000000.0, 1.9999999999999996e+16, -5.999999999999999e+24, 2.4e+33]

The current implementation of `DivBackward0` could not calculate the results correctly even with `1e-8` for triple backward, even though the actual result still within the `float32` range.

## Expected behavior

See above.

## Environment

 - PyTorch Version (e.g., 1.0): PyTorch 1.6.0
 - OS (e.g., Linux): Ubuntu
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): `conda`
 - Build command you used (if compiling from source): N/A
 - Python version: 3.8
 - CUDA/cuDNN version: N/A
 - GPU models and configuration: N/A
 - Any other relevant information: N/A

## Additional context

<!-- Add any other context about the problem here. -->

[albanD]: Hi,

If you remove the squaring in the division then the formula is not correct anymore right? Or do you update anything else to keep that formula correct?

---

[mfkasim1]: Those formulas are equal to each other.
The original formula is `-grad * self / (other * other)`, and I just substitute `self / other = result`, so it equals to `-grad * result / other`.
Another alternative is `-grad * (self / other) / other`, but it has more operations than the previous one.

---

[albanD]: Ho I didn't see the result change there!
What kind of errors are you seeing? Variables being modified inplace? or gradient checks failing?

---

[mfkasim1]: All of them are variables being modified inplace. I guess the formula `-grad * result / other` will introduce BC breaking.

However, when I use `-grad * (self / other) / other` formula, it can pass all the autograd tests successfully (same status with the previous implementation).
So now I think it is up to PyTorch's team to choose between:

1. `-grad * self / (other * other)`
2. `-grad * (self / other) / other`

The first one might be slightly faster (because the use of multiplication instead of division), but the second one provides better numerical stability.

---

[albanD]: > All of them are variables being modified inplace. I guess the formula -grad * result / other will introduce BC breaking.

Yes... the problem is that if you use "result" in the formula, it has to be saved. And if anything changes the result inplace later, it will raise an error.

> the second one provides better numerical stability.

In your example of multiple backward passes, how much better is it? I wouldn't expect the slowdown to be problematic here.

---

[mfkasim1]: > In your example of multiple backward passes, how much better is it? I wouldn't expect the slowdown to be problematic here.

Here's the example above in case of `y=a/b` where `a=b=tensor(1e-8)` (I paste it here to make it easier to read):

      y ,   grad(y,b) , grad(grad(y,b),b)   , grad^3(y,b)            , grad^4(y,b)

    Div1 (current implementation):

    Div2 (proposed implementation):
    [1.0, -100000000.0, 2.000000054512845e+16, -6.000000083090567e+24, 2.4000002343777533e+33]
    Actual:
    [1.0, -100000000.0, 1.9999999999999996e+16, -5.999999999999999e+24, 2.4e+33]

1. The first grads are exactly the same
1. For the second grads, the relative error for the current implementation is about `8.0e-8` while for the proposed implementation it is about `2.7e-8` (the errors are still small, but the error for the proposed implementation is lower).
1. For the third and fourth grads, the current implementation already gives `-inf` and `nan` while the actual result (and the proposed implementation) is still within the `float32` range

---

[mfkasim1]: I have just made a more thorough comparison between the current implementation and the new implementation [here](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1XEkZNputspFHfIQkRFPWFImF0PpW-F_d?usp=sharing).
The conclusions are:

1. The higher order grads for the current implementation can produces `nan` and `inf` while the proposed implementation only produces `inf`.
2. The current implementation results in more anomalies (`nan` and `inf`) than the proposed implementation.
3. There is **no** case where the proposed implementation produces anomaly and the current implementation does not produce anomaly.

---

[albanD]: Hi,

Thanks for the notebook!
I had a chat with people closer to perf questions and it should be ok to replace the multiplication with a division.
A simple sanity check with a `timeit` benchmark on cpu before and after the change should be fine to make sure it does not significantly slow down the backward pass for a the div op.

I'll check that and get back to you.

stage1.title: License file in wheels and conda packages does not contain any third-party licenses
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

License files for relevant code that's used or linked to must be distributed with binaries. There are many license files in `third_party` that must be distributed together with any source or binary distribution.

This was noticed by the conda-forge team in https://github.com/conda-forge/pytorch-cpu-feedstock/issues/34

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Download a wheel from, e.g., https://pypi.org/project/torch/1.7.1/#files
2. Unpack it (it's just a zipfile)
3. Inspect the license file in the `torch-1.7.0.dist-info` directory - it's only a copy of https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/LICENSE. No other license files (there are many in `third_party/` are mentioned or present anywhere in the package.


## Expected behavior

The correct way of dealing with this is normally:

- Keep the main `LICENSE` file in the root of the repo unchanged (the default license for new code contributed to the project).
- Keep a separate list of license files present in the repo, in a script or metadata file
- At build time - for any sdist, wheel or conda package - concatenate all those license files together into a single `LICENSE` file. If desired separating the main license from the rest with a _"licenses for bundled code"_ section header.
- Insert that generated license file in the artifacts.

Also, given how often dependencies get added or changed in `third_party`, add some kind of a check that all files named `LICENSE`, `LICENSE.*` or `COPYING` are actually included.



cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @bdhirsh @jbschlosser @seemethere @malfet @walterddr

stage1.title: Fix exception chaining all over the codebase
stage1.body:
I would like to suggest a small fix in the way that Python 3's exception chaining is used.

As described in detail in [this article](https://blog.ram.rachum.com/post/621791438475296768/improving-python-exception-chaining-with), exception chaining ([PEP 3134](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-3134/)) can be used to make exceptions more user-friendly, and in that case, the syntax `raise new_exception from old_exception` needs to be used.

For example, the following should be used to chain exceptions:
```python
try:
    something_which_raises_TypeError
except TypeError as e:
    raise ValueError("A more user-friendly exception message.") from e
```
instead of:
```python
try:
    something_which_raises_TypeError
except TypeError:
    raise ValueError("A more user-friendly exception message.")
```

One example which needs to be fixed is:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c7787f7fbf388f9fe326d581726e7ef3f2dce74b/torch/jit/annotations.py#L32-L35

I'd be happy to PR! Let me know your thoughts on this!

As described in detail in [this article](https://blog.ram.rachum.com/post/621791438475296768/improving-python-exception-chaining-with), exception chaining ([PEP 3134](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-3134/)) can be used to make exceptions more user-friendly, and in that case, the syntax `raise new_exception from old_exception` needs to be used.

For example, the following should be used to chain exceptions:
```python
try:
    something_which_raises_TypeError
except TypeError as e:
    raise ValueError("A more user-friendly exception message.") from e
```
instead of:
```python
try:
    something_which_raises_TypeError
except TypeError:
    raise ValueError("A more user-friendly exception message.")
```

One example which needs to be fixed is:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c7787f7fbf388f9fe326d581726e7ef3f2dce74b/torch/jit/annotations.py#L32-L35

I'd be happy to PR! Let me know your thoughts on this!
stage3_gold.comments:
[malfet]: Thank you for suggestion @akihironitta !
Please feel free to write a PR and I will be happy to review it.
Also consider eliminating all calls to that macro with direct `raise .. from ..` calls:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/20abfc21e41dfe0bd2500295f7482edbeb6b6c05/torch/_six.py#L56-L60

Although not all instances require exception chaining, for example implicit chaining is totally fine in cases that you've mentioned in the issue description:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c7787f7fbf388f9fe326d581726e7ef3f2dce74b/torch/jit/annotations.py#L32-L35

---

[akihironitta]: Thank you for your quick response.

Sure, I'll remove `raise_from()` and use `raise .. from ..` instead all over the codebase.

> Although not all instances require exception chaining, for example implicit chaining is totally fine in cases that you've mentioned in the issue description:
> https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c7787f7fbf388f9fe326d581726e7ef3f2dce74b/torch/jit/annotations.py#L32-L35

I agree that not all instances require exception chaining. However, I think we should not use implicit chaining in the above case because its error message `During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred` is confusing.

For example, if we run the script below (`test.py`):
```python
d = {"dog": 1}
key = "cat"
try: 
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
except KeyError:
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key))
```
it'll give us an error message like this:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 4, in <module>
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
KeyError: 'cat'

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 6, in <module>
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key))
RuntimeError: no member called cat
```

`During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred` is somewhat confusing when debugging because the truth is that another exception occurred to explain the first exception (`KeyError` in this case) in a friendlier way, not because another **unexpected** exception occured while handling the first exception.

In order to fix confusing messages like this, one option is:
```python
try: 
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
except KeyError as e:
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key)) from e
```
which outputs
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 4, in <module>
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
KeyError: 'cat'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 6, in <module>
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key)) from e
RuntimeError: no member called cat
```

However, in this case, the above message is a bit noisy and redundant.
If we want to suppress the first error message, we should use `raise .. from None` so as to suppress the first exception message (see [Suppress Context in PEP 3134](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-3134/#open-issue-suppressing-context)).
```python
try: 
    print(d[key])  # raises KeyError
except KeyError:
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key)) from None
```
which outputs
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/nitta/tmp/test.py", line 6, in <module>
    raise RuntimeError("no member called {}".format(key)) from None
RuntimeError: no member called cat
```

Do you think using `raise .. from None` is reasonable in the below case or simliar cases?
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c7787f7fbf388f9fe326d581726e7ef3f2dce74b/torch/jit/annotations.py#L32-L35

---

[akihironitta]: ~As there seems a lot of places (over 100 places in this repo) to check, it may be a good idea to label this issue as `good first issue` for people who are interested in contributing. It can also make each PR relatively small. What do you think? (I can work on this issue by myself, but it might take some time...)~ I think I can handle this by myself.

---

[akihironitta]: @malfet Thanks for your response the other day. As I checked and fixed all the files under `torch/` directory, could you have a look at #43836?

---

[malfet]: @akihironitta left a few comments on the PR, but overall looks good!

---

[akihironitta]: @malfet Thank you for reviewing the changes! I've just fixed them reflecting your code.

stage1.title: ConvTranspose2d much slower with output_padding set
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

A `nn.ConvTranspose2d` can be up to two orders of magnitude slower when the `output_padding` option is set to a nonzero value then when it isn't.

## To Reproduce

```
class Test(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, output_padding):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.c1 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(128, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
        self.c2 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
        self.c3 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 3, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.c1(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        x = self.c2(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        x = self.c3(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        return x

def test(output_padding):
    network = Test(output_padding=output_padding).cuda()
    x = torch.rand((1028, 128, 6, 6)).cuda()


    for i in range(5):
        start = time.time()
        for i in range(10):
            network(x)
        print((time.time() - start) / 10)

test((0, 0))
test((1, 1))
```

On my V100 machine, I get timings of about 0.0004s per forward pass with `output_padding=(0, 0)` and about .05s with `output_padding=(1, 1)`.

## Expected behavior

Given that the `output_padding` option has minimal effect on the number of FLOPs required to compute the function, I would expect the computation time to be similar with and without the option.



## Environment

stage3_gold.comments:
[ngimel]: This likely happens because cudnn is not used for convolutions with non-zero `output_padding`, which in turn is a result of this check 
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/22d84204f7188ed4042505e723eef46f048ff47c/aten/src/ATen/native/Convolution.cpp#L96-L102
This check was added because wrong results/CUDNN_STATUS_BAD_PARAMS were produced in some similar cases, but maybe the check is unnecessarily strict. 
Looks like `output_padding[i] >= dilation[i]` will be true for most cases. T
@ptrblck, @csarofeen to check if it is still a real limitation for cudnn, or if this check can be relaxed.

---

[linjiapro]: @xwang233 @ngimel  thanks for investigating and fixing this. I am experiencing exactly the same issue.

---

[linjiapro]: This is my temporary workaround for this issue. 
There is a formula about how to calculate output size:
https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.ConvTranspose2d.html

In real usage cases, the output size and input size are usually fixed, and we need to tune the padding, dilation, etc. We can set output_padding = 0, and design other parameters to make sure output size and input size are fit. In my case, I changed kernel size to match input/.output size while having output_padding = 0.

stage1.title: Segfault with nightly in python 3.9
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

A simple code segfaults in nightly builds with python 3.9 but works with python 3.8
## To Reproduce
Content of `Dockerfile`:
```
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster
# works with 3.8
USER root
WORKDIR /root
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install git build-essential --yes
RUN python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip
RUN python3 -m pip install --pre torch==1.8.0.dev20210102+cpu  -f https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cpu/torch_nightly.html
RUN python3 -m pip install Pillow
RUN git clone https://github.com/pytorch/vision/
ENV PYTHONPATH=./vision
COPY test-backbone.py /
RUN python /test-backbone.py
```

Content of `test-backbone.py`:
```
from torchvision.models import resnet50
import torch


if __name__ == "__main__":
    backbone = resnet50(pretrained=True)

    img = torch.randn((2, 3, 256, 288))
    features = backbone(img)
    loss = features.sum()
    loss.backward()
    print("exiting")
```

Run `docker build  -t py39:v0 .`

Logs:
```
Step 11/11 : RUN python /test-backbone.py
 ---> Running in 31a88ed05b3d
Downloading: "https://download.pytorch.org/models/resnet50-19c8e357.pth" to /root/.cache/torch/hub/checkpoints/resnet50-19c8e357.pth
100.0%
exiting
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
The command '/bin/sh -c python /test-backbone.py' returned a non-zero code: 139

```

stage1.title: cuSPARSE handle is not thread-safe
stage1.body:
From what I observe when working on https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/29233, cusparse handle is managed the same way as cublas handle, therefore not thread-safe.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/29233 makes the handle pool mechanism which was originally used for cudnn generic, so it would also be able to use to manage cusparse handle. We should migrate the management of cusparse handle to that approach.

See also: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/6962

stage1.title: Improvement of autograd engine original task placement in worker threads
stage1.body:
Currently, when a call to the autograd engine is done, the original task is always placed on the CPU worker queue.
While this works great, it can lead to surprising behavior, in particular when re-entrant autograd happen from a GPU thread.

Indeed, even though the whole code runs on a GPU and should run serially on the GPU thread, the original task happening on the CPU can lead to non-determinism and bad ordering of the execution (which can lead to very bad memory usage when using checkpointing and independent branches).

From the top of my head, I think we should:
- Remove [this code](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/4fc525e72976a470ca7a56264734c3cb0afe1fe8/torch/csrc/autograd/engine.cpp#L867) when there is a single input: we can just use that input's grad_fn as the graph root. That will be better perf-wise, especially for very small graphs.
- Change [this code](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/4fc525e72976a470ca7a56264734c3cb0afe1fe8/torch/csrc/autograd/engine.cpp#L892-L893) to push on the right queue based on the inputs (mimicking the logic [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/4fc525e72976a470ca7a56264734c3cb0afe1fe8/torch/csrc/autograd/input_buffer.cpp#L121-L137)).

Even though I wouldn't expect anyone to rely on this, this would be BC-breaking. But I think the determinism and gain in memory in these cases will be worth it.

cc @ezyang @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @pearu @nikitaved @gchanan @SsnL

stage1.title: autograd.grad with set_detect_anomaly(True) will cause memory leak
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

using `torch.autograd.grad()` with `torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True)` will cause memory leak

## To Reproduce

Run the code snippet below.
It will have about 2MiB GPU memory consumption increasing each iteration.

If comment out the `set_detect_anomaly` line, then there is no memory leak, with constant memory consumption.

```python
import torch
torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) # if comment out this, no leak
for rep in range(1000):
    batch = torch.ones(10, 30000).cuda().requires_grad_()
    y=batch.norm()
    grad = torch.autograd.grad(
        outputs=y, inputs=batch,
        create_graph=True, retain_graph=True, only_inputs=True)[0]
    print("memory allocated:", float(torch.cuda.memory_allocated()/1024**2), "MiB")
    pass
```

## Expected behavior

No memory leak with or without `set_detect_anomaly(True)`

## Environment

 - PyTorch Version: 1.7.1
 - OS: Linux
 - How you installed PyTorch: conda, source: `-c pytorch`
 - Python version: 3.8.5
 - CUDA/cuDNN version: cuda11.0

## Additional context

BTW, if replace `y=batch.norm()` with `y=batch.mean()`, then there is no memory leak with or without `set_detect_anomaly`, which makes me very confused.


cc @ezyang @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @pearu @nikitaved @soulitzer

stage1.title: torch.gradient currently only supports edge_order to be equal to one.
stage1.body:
Numpy gradient function is able to support edge_order to be either equal to one or two:
https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.gradient.html

However, currently PyTorch only supports edge_order to be only equal to one.  Adding a feature of supporting edge_order to be equal to two, would conclude to domains of arguments in Numpy and PyTorch to be matched.

stage1.title: Noisy warning raised by 'default_collate'
stage1.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

After upgrading pytorch version from 1.10.1 to the master branch (commit [d697bb4](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/commit/d697bb4220ff5ea8b46591cc082583bbf1a294a4)), `torch.utils.data._utils.collate.default_collate` raises the below noisy warning repeatedly:

```
UserWarning: An output with one or more elements was resized since it had shape [10], which does not
match the required output shape [2, 5].This behavior is deprecated, and in a future PyTorch release outputs will
not be resized unless they have zero elements. You can explicitly reuse an out tensor t by resizing it, inplace,
to zero elements with t.resize_(0).
```
The warning is original from [Resize.cpp](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/Resize.cpp#L11-L27) and triggered by [these lines](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/utils/data/_utils/collate.py#L130-L138) of `default_colloate`:

```
    elem = batch[0]
    elem_type = type(elem)
    if isinstance(elem, torch.Tensor):
        out = None
        if torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() is not None:
            # If we're in a background process, concatenate directly into a
            # shared memory tensor to avoid an extra copy
            numel = sum(x.numel() for x in batch)
            storage = elem.storage()._new_shared(numel)
            out = elem.new(storage)
        return torch.stack(batch, 0, out=out)
```

In case `default_collate` runs in background/worker process (torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() returns something), `out` is always a 1D tensor, but `batch` may has higher rank, thus a resize operation happens inside the `torch.stack` operation, which triggers the warning.

### Versions

Master branch (commit [d697bb4](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/commit/d697bb4220ff5ea8b46591cc082583bbf1a294a4))

# To Reproduce
Use this code snippet to reproduce the problem:

```
import torch

a, b = torch.randn([5]), torch.randn([5])
batch = [a, b]
elem = batch[0]

# In case torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() is not None
numel = sum(x.numel() for x in batch)
storage = elem.storage()._new_shared(numel)
out = elem.new(storage)

torch.stack(batch, 0, out=out)
```

# Expected behavior
No warning raises.

# Workaround

```
    elem = batch[0]
    elem_type = type(elem)
    if isinstance(elem, torch.Tensor):
        out = None
        if torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() is not None:
            # If we're in a background process, concatenate directly into a
            # shared memory tensor to avoid an extra copy
            numel = sum(x.numel() for x in batch)
            storage = elem.storage()._new_shared(numel)

            # reshape `out` before passing to torch.stack
            out = elem.new(storage).view(-1, *list(elem.size()))  

        return torch.stack(batch, 0, out=out)
```

Test code:

```
import torch

a, b = torch.randn([5]), torch.randn([5])
batch = [a, b]
elem = batch[0]

# In case torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() is not None
numel = sum(x.numel() for x in batch)
storage = elem.storage()._new_shared(numel)
out = elem.new(storage).view(-1, *list(elem.size()))

torch.stack(batch, 0, out=out)
```

stage3_gold.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

After upgrading pytorch version from 1.10.1 to the master branch (commit [d697bb4](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/commit/d697bb4220ff5ea8b46591cc082583bbf1a294a4)), `torch.utils.data._utils.collate.default_collate` raises the below noisy warning repeatedly:

```
UserWarning: An output with one or more elements was resized since it had shape [10], which does not
match the required output shape [2, 5].This behavior is deprecated, and in a future PyTorch release outputs will
not be resized unless they have zero elements. You can explicitly reuse an out tensor t by resizing it, inplace,
to zero elements with t.resize_(0).
```
The warning is original from [Resize.cpp](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/Resize.cpp#L11-L27) and triggered by [these lines](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/utils/data/_utils/collate.py#L130-L138) of `default_colloate`:

```
    elem = batch[0]
    elem_type = type(elem)
    if isinstance(elem, torch.Tensor):
        out = None
        if torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() is not None:
            # If we're in a background process, concatenate directly into a
            # shared memory tensor to avoid an extra copy
            numel = sum(x.numel() for x in batch)
            storage = elem.storage()._new_shared(numel)
            out = elem.new(storage)
        return torch.stack(batch, 0, out=out)
```

In case `default_collate` runs in background/worker process (torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() returns something), `out` is always a 1D tensor, but `batch` may has higher rank, thus a resize operation happens inside the `torch.stack` operation, which triggers the warning.

### Versions

Master branch (commit [d697bb4](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/commit/d697bb4220ff5ea8b46591cc082583bbf1a294a4))

# To Reproduce
Use this code snippet to reproduce the problem:

```
import torch

a, b = torch.randn([5]), torch.randn([5])
batch = [a, b]
elem = batch[0]

# In case torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() is not None
numel = sum(x.numel() for x in batch)
storage = elem.storage()._new_shared(numel)
out = elem.new(storage)

torch.stack(batch, 0, out=out)
```

# Expected behavior
No warning raises.

# Workaround

```
    elem = batch[0]
    elem_type = type(elem)
    if isinstance(elem, torch.Tensor):
        out = None
        if torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() is not None:
            # If we're in a background process, concatenate directly into a
            # shared memory tensor to avoid an extra copy
            numel = sum(x.numel() for x in batch)
            storage = elem.storage()._new_shared(numel)

            # reshape `out` before passing to torch.stack
            out = elem.new(storage).view(-1, *list(elem.size()))  

        return torch.stack(batch, 0, out=out)
```

Test code:

```
import torch

a, b = torch.randn([5]), torch.randn([5])
batch = [a, b]
elem = batch[0]

# In case torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() is not None
numel = sum(x.numel() for x in batch)
storage = elem.storage()._new_shared(numel)
out = elem.new(storage).view(-1, *list(elem.size()))

torch.stack(batch, 0, out=out)
```

cc @VitalyFedyunin @ejguan @NivekT

stage1.title: Run time error with backward()  after upgrading to pytorch 1.2.0
stage1.body:
## 🐛 Bug

The following error occurs after I upgrade to Pytorch 1.2.0. 
one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified by an inplace operation: [torch.FloatTensor [3]], which is output 0 of AddBackward0, is at version 1; expected version 0 instead.

## To Reproduce

Here are my codes. They work fine in Pytorch 1.1.0.

import torch

b0 = torch.tensor(5.0, requires_grad = True)
a = torch.Tensor([1,0,0])
b = torch.zeros(3, requires_grad = True)
c = torch.ones(3, requires_grad = True)

bb = b+1

bb[a!=0] = torch.min(bb[a!=0], c[a!=0])

d = torch.sum(bb)
d.backward()

## Expected behavior

It should run with no error.

## Environment

torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) shows that error is with the following line.

bb[a!=0] = torch.min(bb[a!=0], c[a!=0])

 - PyTorch Version: 1.2.0
 - OS (e.g., Linux): Windows 10
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): conda
 - Build command you used (if compiling from source):
 - Python version: 3.7.3
 - CUDA/cuDNN version: None


cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @SsnL @albanD

stage1.title: Add kernel version and glibc version to collect_env
stage1.body:
## 🚀 Feature

TensorPipe uses some advanced features of the Linux kernel. It does so on a "best effort" basis (i.e., use them if available, fall back on something else if not). This logic is unfortunately hard to test because it would require specific kernel versions on our CI machines. So it occasionally happens that we find out about issues when users report them. To help investigate these reports we've found it useful to know the kernel version and the glibc version used by the user (both when building and when running, if they're different). It would be great if these could be added to the report produced by collect_env.
